items.objective: Screen for intracranial aneurysm with MR angiography in ADPKD with a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old man with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease diagnosed by ultrasonography has blood pressure of 146/94 mm Hg, 148/92 mm Hg and 150/96 mm Hg at three visits over 2 months despite reducing his salt intake. He takes no medications. Serum potassium is 4.3 mEq/L and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 40 mg/g. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Hypertension in ADPKD is driven by activation of the renin-angiotensin system, and an ACE inhibitor (or an angiotensin receptor blocker if not tolerated) is first line. It lowers blood pressure, reduces albuminuria and, with tight control in young patients with preserved GFR, slows the growth in kidney volume. Potassium and creatinine should be checked after starting.

Takeaway: ACE inhibitor or ARB first for hypertension in ADPKD.

whyNot.A: Calcium channel blockers lower pressure but do not target the RAAS-driven mechanism or albuminuria and are second line.
whyNot.B: Thiazides are add-on agents; they can cause hypokalemia, which may promote cyst growth.
whyNot.D: Beta-blockers are not first line for uncomplicated hypertension in ADPKD.
whyNot.E: Tolvaptan slows cyst growth in rapidly progressive disease but is not an antihypertensive.

items.objective: Choose an ACE inhibitor or ARB as first-line treatment for hypertension in ADPKD.

items.stemHtml:
A 37-year-old woman with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (PKD1 variant) has the following results over 3 years:

YeareGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²)Total kidney volume on MRI (mL)
1841,450
2771,640
3691,860

Her kidney volume places her in the highest-risk class for her age. Blood pressure is 116/74 mm Hg on losartan. She drinks about 3 L of water daily and follows a low-sodium diet. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
She has rapidly progressive ADPKD: a large and growing total kidney volume for her age and a loss of about 7–8 mL/min/1.73 m² per year. The vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist tolvaptan slows the growth in kidney volume and the decline in eGFR in such patients, and is indicated in addition to blood pressure control, water intake and sodium restriction.

Takeaway: add tolvaptan for adults with ADPKD at risk of rapid progression.

whyNot.A: mTOR inhibitors did not slow kidney function loss in ADPKD trials and cause significant adverse effects.
whyNot.B: Loop diuretics do not slow cyst growth and could cause volume depletion and a fall in GFR.
whyNot.C: Somatostatin analogues can reduce liver cyst volume but are not the standard agent for slowing kidney decline.
whyNot.D: Adding a mineralocorticoid antagonist to an ARB raises the risk of hyperkalemia and is not a disease-modifying ADPKD therapy.

items.objective: Identify rapidly progressive ADPKD and add tolvaptan.

items.stemHtml: The patient starts tolvaptan. She is told to expect increased thirst and urination. Which of the following tests must be monitored regularly because of a serious adverse effect of this drug?
items.explanationHtml:
Tolvaptan can cause idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury, sometimes severe. Liver tests (ALT, AST and bilirubin) are checked before starting and then regularly, most often monthly for the first 18 months and less often afterwards, and the drug is stopped if they rise. Sodium also deserves attention because aquaresis can cause hypernatremia if she cannot drink enough.

Takeaway: monitor liver tests on tolvaptan.

whyNot.A: Tolvaptan does not cause marrow suppression.
whyNot.C: Myopathy with raised creatine kinase is a statin adverse effect, not a tolvaptan one.
whyNot.D: Pancreatitis is not a recognised tolvaptan toxicity requiring monitoring.
whyNot.E: Thyroid dysfunction is caused by drugs such as lithium and amiodarone, not tolvaptan.

items.objective: Monitor liver tests during tolvaptan therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and an eGFR of 48 mL/min/1.73 m² has had fever to 38.9°C (102°F) and constant left flank pain for 4 days. Urinalysis shows 3–5 white blood cells per high-power field; urine culture from 2 days ago is negative. Blood cultures grow E. coli. MRI shows a 4-cm left renal cyst with a thickened wall and layering debris, consistent with an infected cyst. He has received intravenous ceftriaxone for 72 hours and remains febrile. Which of the following is the most appropriate change in antibiotic therapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Infected cysts in ADPKD often have negative urine cultures because they do not communicate with the collecting system. Lipid-soluble antibiotics that penetrate the cyst wall, such as fluoroquinolones (or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), are preferred; beta-lactams penetrate cysts poorly, which explains his persistent fever. Treatment usually lasts several weeks, and a large cyst that still does not respond is drained percutaneously.

Takeaway: treat ADPKD cyst infection with a cyst-penetrating antibiotic such as a fluoroquinolone.

whyNot.A: Vancomycin covers gram-positive organisms and adds nothing against E. coli.
whyNot.B: Cefazolin is another beta-lactam with poor cyst penetration and narrower gram-negative activity.
whyNot.D: Nitrofurantoin reaches only the urine; it has no useful blood or tissue levels and cannot treat bacteremia or cyst infection.
whyNot.E: Continuing a drug that penetrates the cyst poorly while he stays febrile risks treatment failure.

items.objective: Treat infected renal cysts in ADPKD with a lipid-soluble, cyst-penetrating antibiotic.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman with tuberous sclerosis complex is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the sudden onset of severe right flank pain while lifting a box. She is pale and diaphoretic. Pulse is 128/min and blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg; after 2 L of crystalloid and 2 units of packed red cells, blood pressure is 100/62 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL. CT angiography shows a 9-cm fat-containing right renal mass with a large perirenal hematoma and active contrast extravasation from a branch of the renal artery. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage from a large angiomyolipoma (Wunderlich syndrome) is the tumour's main danger. In a patient who responds to resuscitation, selective arterial embolisation stops the bleeding and preserves kidney tissue, which matters in tuberous sclerosis because tumours are often bilateral and recur. Surgery is kept for failure of embolisation or uncontrollable instability.

Takeaway: bleeding angiomyolipoma: resuscitate, then selective arterial embolisation.

whyNot.A: Radical nephrectomy removes the whole kidney, which is unnecessary when embolisation can control bleeding and harmful in a patient prone to bilateral tumours.
whyNot.B: Active extravasation with hypotension needs intervention, not observation.
whyNot.C: Fat on CT already makes the diagnosis; biopsy would add bleeding risk and delay treatment.
whyNot.E: Everolimus shrinks angiomyolipomas over months and has no role in acute hemorrhage.

items.objective: Treat acute hemorrhage from a renal angiomyolipoma with selective arterial embolisation.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old woman in good health has renal ultrasonography for microscopic hematuria, which shows a complex cystic lesion in the left kidney. Renal-protocol CT shows a 3-cm cyst in the lower pole with a thick, irregular wall and a 9-mm soft-tissue nodule along the wall that enhances after contrast. There is no lymphadenopathy, and the chest radiograph is normal. Her serum creatinine is 0.7 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Aspiration of the cyst fluid for cytology

options.label: E
options.html: Radical nephrectomy with regional lymph node dissection

items.explanationHtml:
An enhancing soft-tissue nodule within a cyst makes it Bosniak IV, which carries a high probability of cystic renal cell carcinoma. In a healthy patient with a small lesion, partial (nephron-sparing) nephrectomy removes the tumour with clear margins while preserving kidney function.

Takeaway: Bosniak IV (and most III) cysts are treated as cancer; prefer partial nephrectomy for small lesions.

whyNot.A: Cyst aspiration has poor sensitivity for carcinoma and risks spilling tumour cells.
whyNot.B: Surveillance suits Bosniak IIF cysts, or small III/IV lesions in patients who cannot tolerate surgery; she is healthy.
whyNot.C: Ignoring an enhancing nodule would leave a probable cancer untreated.
whyNot.E: Radical nephrectomy removes more kidney than needed for a 3-cm lesion, and node dissection is not routine without nodal disease.

items.objective: Treat a Bosniak IV renal cyst with partial nephrectomy in a fit patient.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man has had headaches and unsteady gait for 2 months. MRI of the brain shows a cystic cerebellar mass with an enhancing mural nodule. Ophthalmoscopy shows a vascular retinal tumour. CT of the abdomen shows several solid enhancing masses in both kidneys and multiple renal and pancreatic cysts. His father had a kidney removed for cancer at age 39. Loss of the protein encoded by the gene most likely mutated in this patient causes tumour growth mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Accumulation of hypoxia-inducible factor under normal oxygen tension

options.label: B
options.html: Constitutive activation of the MET receptor tyrosine kinase

options.label: C
options.html: Failure to repair DNA base mismatches

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of the Rb-mediated G1 cell-cycle checkpoint

options.label: E
options.html: Unrestrained mTORC1 activity from loss of the hamartin-tuberin complex

items.explanationHtml:
Cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas, pancreatic cysts and bilateral early renal tumours in a family is von Hippel-Lindau disease. The VHL protein is part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase that marks HIF for proteasomal degradation when oxygen is present. Without it, HIF accumulates and drives VEGF and other angiogenic genes, producing highly vascular tumours such as clear cell renal cell carcinoma.

Takeaway: VHL loss stabilises HIF, causing angiogenesis and clear cell RCC.

whyNot.B: Activating MET mutations cause hereditary papillary renal carcinoma without hemangioblastomas.
whyNot.C: Mismatch repair defects (Lynch syndrome) cause colon, endometrial and upper-tract urothelial cancers.
whyNot.D: Rb loss causes retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma; retinal hemangioblastoma is a different, vascular tumour.
whyNot.E: Loss of hamartin or tuberin is tuberous sclerosis, which causes angiomyolipomas rather than hemangioblastomas.

items.objective: Explain how VHL loss causes clear cell renal cell carcinoma through HIF accumulation.

items.stemHtml:
A 66-year-old man has 3 weeks of constipation, thirst and confusion. He has smoked for 45 years. CT shows an 8-cm solid, enhancing mass in the right kidney and no bone lesions. Laboratory studies show:

TestResult
Calcium, total13.4 mg/dL
Phosphorus2.2 mg/dL
Parathyroid hormone8 pg/mL (N = 10–65)
25-hydroxyvitamin D32 ng/mL (N = 30–100)

Which of the following is the most likely cause of his hypercalcemia?
items.explanationHtml:
A large renal mass with hypercalcemia, low phosphorus and a suppressed PTH without bone metastases is humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy. Renal cell carcinoma commonly secretes PTH-related peptide, which binds the PTH receptor in bone and kidney, raising bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption and causing phosphaturia. Normal PTH physiology then shuts PTH off.

Takeaway: hypercalcemia with low PTH and a renal mass means PTHrP from renal cell carcinoma.

whyNot.A: Calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia is typical of lymphoma and granulomatous disease; renal cell carcinoma does not usually work this way.
whyNot.B: True ectopic PTH secretion is extremely rare, and PTH here is suppressed.
whyNot.C: CT shows no bone lesions; local osteolysis is more typical of myeloma and breast cancer.
whyNot.D: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes high or inappropriately normal PTH, not suppressed PTH.

items.objective: Recognise PTH-related peptide secretion by renal cell carcinoma as a cause of hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man has noticed a soft, painless swelling in the left scrotum for 3 weeks. Examination while standing shows a mass of dilated, tortuous veins above the left testis; it does not decrease in size when he lies flat. The right side is normal. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

options.label: A
options.html: Compression of the left common iliac vein by the right common iliac artery

options.label: B
options.html: Incompetent valves in the left internal spermatic vein

options.label: D
options.html: Obstruction of the left renal vein by tumour

options.label: E
options.html: Thrombosis of the inferior vena cava below the renal veins

items.explanationHtml:
The left gonadal (testicular) vein drains into the left renal vein, whereas the right drains directly into the inferior vena cava. A new left varicocele in an older man that does not empty when he lies down suggests obstruction of venous outflow, classically renal cell carcinoma growing into the left renal vein. It should prompt renal imaging.

Takeaway: a new left varicocele that persists supine in an older man means look for a left renal mass.

whyNot.A: Compression of the left common iliac vein (May-Thurner) causes left leg swelling and DVT, not a varicocele.
whyNot.B: Valve incompetence causes the common idiopathic varicocele of adolescents, which empties when lying down.
whyNot.C: Torsion is acutely painful with a high-riding, tender testis, not a painless bag of veins.
whyNot.E: Infrarenal caval thrombosis would cause bilateral leg edema and, if anything, right-sided or bilateral changes.

items.objective: Link a nondecompressing left varicocele to obstruction of the left renal vein by renal cell carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for a large abdominal mass found by his mother while bathing him. He was born without irises and has hypospadias and an undescended testis; his developmental milestones have been delayed. Examination shows a smooth, firm left flank mass that does not cross the midline. Blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg. Which of the following genetic abnormalities is most likely present?
items.explanationHtml:
Aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, developmental delay and a renal mass make up WAGR syndrome. It is caused by a contiguous deletion at 11p13 that removes PAX6 (aniridia) and the tumour suppressor WT1 (Wilms tumour and genital anomalies). The mass is a Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma).

Takeaway: WAGR = 11p13 deletion of WT1 and PAX6.

whyNot.A: MYCN amplification marks aggressive neuroblastoma, an adrenal tumour that often crosses the midline.
whyNot.C: Imprinting defects at 11p15.5 cause Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (macroglossia, omphalocele, overgrowth), not aniridia.
whyNot.D: Loss of 3p is the signature of clear cell renal carcinoma in adults.
whyNot.E: Trisomy 18 causes clenched hands, rocker-bottom feet and heart defects, and few patients survive infancy.

items.objective: Identify WAGR syndrome and its 11p13 deletion as a cause of Wilms tumour.

items.stemHtml: A 2-day-old girl born at 39 weeks weighs 4,700 g (above the 97th percentile). She has a large protruding tongue, a small omphalocele and an enlarged left arm and leg. Her blood glucose is 32 mg/dL. Which of the following best describes the genetic basis of her condition and the tumour she must be screened for?

options.label: A
options.html: Abnormal imprinting at 11p15.5 with IGF2 overexpression; Wilms tumour

options.label: C
options.html: Germline VHL mutation; clear cell renal cell carcinoma

items.explanationHtml:
Macrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele, lateralised overgrowth and neonatal hypoglycemia are Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. It results from abnormal imprinting at 11p15.5 (for example loss of maternal methylation, paternal uniparental disomy), which commonly causes overexpression of the growth factor IGF2. Children are at increased risk of embryonal tumours, especially Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma, and are screened with regular abdominal ultrasound.

Takeaway: Beckwith-Wiedemann is an 11p15.5 imprinting disorder that predisposes to Wilms tumour.

whyNot.B: RB1 mutations cause retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma, not overgrowth or omphalocele.
whyNot.C: VHL disease presents with hemangioblastomas and renal cancer in young adults, not neonatal overgrowth.
whyNot.D: TSC2 mutations cause tuberous sclerosis (seizures, skin lesions, angiomyolipomas).
whyNot.E: Neurofibromatosis type 1 causes café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas, not overgrowth at birth.

items.objective: Recognise Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome as an imprinting disorder at 11p15.5 that predisposes to Wilms tumour.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old woman with granulomatosis with polyangiitis was treated with oral cyclophosphamide for 18 months several years ago. She now has painless gross hematuria. Cystoscopy shows a papillary bladder tumour. Which of the following compounds is most responsible for the bladder toxicity of her past treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Cyclophosphamide is activated in the liver; one of its metabolites, acrolein, is excreted in urine and injures the urothelium. It causes acute hemorrhagic cystitis and raises the long-term risk of urothelial carcinoma, especially after prolonged oral therapy. Vigorous hydration and mesna, which binds acrolein in urine, reduce the risk.

Takeaway: cyclophosphamide's metabolite acrolein causes hemorrhagic cystitis and bladder cancer; mesna protects.

whyNot.B: Aminolevulinic acid accumulates in lead poisoning and acute porphyrias, not with cyclophosphamide.
whyNot.C: Formaldehyde comes from methanol metabolism (to formic acid) and is not the bladder toxin of cyclophosphamide.
whyNot.D: Mesna is the protective agent that binds acrolein; it is not toxic to the bladder.
whyNot.E: Methotrexate polyglutamates are intracellular active forms of methotrexate, a different drug.

items.objective: Identify acrolein as the cyclophosphamide metabolite causing hemorrhagic cystitis and bladder cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman took over-the-counter analgesic combinations containing phenacetin daily for back pain for more than 20 years. Ten years ago she passed tissue fragments in her urine during an episode of flank pain. She now has painless gross hematuria. CT urography shows a filling defect in the right renal pelvis. A tumour of which of the following cell types is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Long-term use of phenacetin-containing analgesic mixtures causes analgesic nephropathy with papillary necrosis (the sloughed papillae she passed) and a markedly raised risk of urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis and ureter. A filling defect in the renal pelvis with hematuria fits an upper-tract urothelial tumour.

Takeaway: phenacetin causes papillary necrosis and upper-tract urothelial carcinoma.

whyNot.A: Collecting duct carcinoma is rare and arises in the medulla rather than as a pelvic filling defect; it is not linked to phenacetin.
whyNot.B: Intercalated cells give rise to oncocytoma and chromophobe carcinoma, which are parenchymal masses.
whyNot.C: Metanephric blastema gives rise to Wilms tumour in children.
whyNot.D: Proximal tubule cells give rise to clear cell and papillary renal cell carcinoma in the cortex, not the pelvis.

items.objective: Associate phenacetin analgesic use with papillary necrosis and urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man has high-grade noninvasive papillary urothelial carcinoma of the bladder with adjacent carcinoma in situ, completely resected transurethrally. He is scheduled for weekly instillations of an agent into the bladder through a catheter for 6 weeks. During treatment he develops dysuria, frequency and low-grade fever, which resolve within 48 hours after each dose. Which of the following best describes the agent and how it works?

options.label: A
options.html: An alkylating agent that cross-links tumour DNA

options.label: B
options.html: An antibody that blocks PD-1 on T cells

options.label: C
options.html: An inhibitor of VEGF receptor tyrosine kinases

options.label: D
options.html: A live attenuated mycobacterium that triggers a local immune response against tumour cells

options.label: E
options.html: A topoisomerase II inhibitor that stops DNA replication

items.explanationHtml:
Intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), a live attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis, is standard after resection of high-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ. It attaches to urothelium and recruits a local inflammatory, largely Th1-type immune response (cytokines, macrophages, T and NK cells) that destroys residual tumour cells. Transient cystitis and low-grade fever are expected; persistent high fever suggests disseminated BCG infection.

Takeaway: intravesical BCG is live M. bovis immunotherapy for high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

whyNot.A: Intravesical alkylating or cytotoxic chemotherapy (for example mitomycin) is used, but this pattern of weekly immunotherapy for carcinoma in situ with febrile cystitis is BCG.
whyNot.B: PD-1 inhibitors are given intravenously, mainly for advanced or BCG-unresponsive disease.
whyNot.C: VEGF receptor inhibitors are oral drugs for metastatic renal cell carcinoma.
whyNot.E: Topoisomerase II inhibitors are cytotoxic drugs given systemically, not live organisms.

items.objective: Describe intravesical BCG as live attenuated M. bovis immunotherapy for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman with metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma starts an oral drug. Over the next 2 months her blood pressure rises from 128/80 to 162/98 mm Hg, she develops painful, thickened skin on her palms and soles, and her urine dipstick shows 2+ protein. TSH rises to 11 μU/mL. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the drug?

options.label: B
options.html: Blockade of CTLA-4 on T cells

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of the VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase

items.explanationHtml:
Clear cell RCC depends on HIF-driven VEGF signalling, and oral VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (sunitinib, pazopanib, axitinib, cabozantinib) are a core treatment. Their class effects follow from blocking VEGF: hypertension and proteinuria (loss of VEGF support for endothelium and podocytes), hand-foot skin reaction, impaired wound healing and, with sunitinib especially, hypothyroidism.

Takeaway: hypertension, proteinuria, hand-foot reaction and hypothyroidism on an oral RCC drug point to a VEGF receptor TKI.

whyNot.A: Androgen receptor antagonists treat prostate cancer and cause gynecomastia and hot flashes.
whyNot.B: CTLA-4 blockers (ipilimumab) are intravenous and cause immune-mediated colitis, hepatitis and hypophysitis, not hand-foot reaction and proteinuria.
whyNot.C: Microtubule inhibitors cause neuropathy and myelosuppression and are not used for RCC.
whyNot.E: Topoisomerase I inhibitors (irinotecan, topotecan) cause diarrhea and myelosuppression and are not RCC drugs.

items.objective: Link the adverse-effect profile of VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors to their use in renal cell carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old man noticed red urine with small clots twice last week. He has no dysuria, fever or flank pain. He has smoked 1 pack daily for 45 years and takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Blood pressure is 134/80 mm Hg. Examination is unremarkable. Urinalysis shows many red blood cells with normal shape, no casts and no protein; urine culture is negative. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Attribute the bleeding to apixaban and repeat urinalysis in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
Gross hematuria without infection is the most important warning sign of urinary tract cancer, and as a long-term smoker he is high risk. He needs a full evaluation of the upper tract with multiphase CT urography and of the bladder with cystoscopy. Anticoagulation does not explain hematuria; it often unmasks an underlying lesion.

Takeaway: gross hematuria, even on anticoagulants, needs CT urography plus cystoscopy.

whyNot.A: Blaming the anticoagulant delays the diagnosis of a possible cancer.
whyNot.C: Ultrasonography misses small upper-tract urothelial tumours and does not assess the bladder adequately; it is for low-risk patients or those who cannot have CT contrast.
whyNot.D: Stopping a needed anticoagulant without evaluation exposes him to stroke and still leaves the cause unknown.
whyNot.E: Cytology has low sensitivity for low-grade tumours and cannot replace imaging and cystoscopy.

items.objective: Evaluate gross hematuria in a high-risk patient with CT urography and cystoscopy.

items.stemHtml: CT urography in the patient shows a 2-cm enhancing lesion on the left lateral bladder wall and normal upper tracts. Transurethral resection removes the tumour completely. Pathology shows high-grade noninvasive papillary urothelial carcinoma (Ta) with adjacent carcinoma in situ; detrusor muscle in the specimen is free of tumour. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Intravesical BCG induction followed by maintenance therapy

options.label: C
options.html: Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy and radical cystectomy

items.explanationHtml:
He has high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (high grade with carcinoma in situ). After complete resection, intravesical BCG, an induction course followed by maintenance instillations, reduces recurrence and progression to muscle invasion. Cystoscopy and cytology surveillance follow; radical cystectomy is reserved for BCG failure or very high-risk features.

Takeaway: high-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer or carcinoma in situ: TURBT then intravesical BCG.

whyNot.A: Radiation is not standard for non-muscle-invasive disease.
whyNot.C: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with cystectomy is the standard for muscle-invasive (T2 or higher) disease, which he does not have.
whyNot.D: Surveillance alone suits low-grade, low-risk tumours; high-grade disease with carcinoma in situ is likely to recur and progress.
whyNot.E: Systemic checkpoint inhibitors are reserved for BCG-unresponsive or advanced disease.

items.objective: Treat high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer with intravesical BCG after TURBT.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has a routine examination before starting a new job. She has no symptoms, takes no medications and has never smoked. A urine dipstick is positive (1+) for blood; she is not menstruating. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Microscopic examination of the urine sediment

items.explanationHtml:
A positive dipstick detects the peroxidase activity of heme, so it is also positive with myoglobin and free hemoglobin. Microscopy is needed to confirm true hematuria (3 or more red cells per high-power field) before any further evaluation. If it is confirmed, the next steps depend on risk; a young, nonsmoking woman with a few red cells is low risk.

Takeaway: confirm a positive dipstick with urine microscopy before working up hematuria.

whyNot.A: CT urography is for confirmed hematuria in higher-risk patients, not an unconfirmed dipstick result.
whyNot.B: Cystoscopy is not indicated before hematuria is confirmed, and she is low risk.
whyNot.D: Biopsy is for suspected glomerular disease with proteinuria, dysmorphic red cells or casts or declining function.
whyNot.E: Cytology is not part of the initial evaluation of microscopic hematuria.

items.objective: Confirm dipstick hematuria with urine microscopy.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old man has CT for diverticulitis that incidentally shows a 2.8-cm solid mass in the lower pole of the right kidney. Renal-protocol CT shows that the mass enhances avidly and contains no fat. There is no renal vein involvement, lymphadenopathy or distant metastasis; chest CT is normal. He is otherwise healthy, and his eGFR is 82 mL/min/1.73 m². Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Active surveillance with CT every 6 months

options.label: E
options.html: Systemic VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor

items.explanationHtml:
An enhancing solid renal mass without fat is presumed to be renal cell carcinoma. For a localised tumour of 4 cm or less (T1a) in a fit patient, partial (nephron-sparing) nephrectomy cures most patients and preserves kidney function, which lowers his later risk of CKD and cardiovascular disease.

Takeaway: small localised renal masses in fit patients: partial nephrectomy.

whyNot.A: Active surveillance suits older or frail patients with small masses; in a healthy 56-year-old it risks progression.
whyNot.C: Radical nephrectomy is for larger or central tumours not amenable to partial resection; here it would sacrifice nephrons unnecessarily.
whyNot.D: Systemic therapy is for metastatic or high-risk disease, not localised small tumours.
whyNot.E: VEGF receptor inhibitors are used for metastatic disease, not as primary treatment of a resectable tumour.

items.objective: Treat a small localised renal mass in a fit patient with partial nephrectomy.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman had a radical nephrectomy for clear cell renal cell carcinoma 2 years ago. She now has a cough and a 5-kg weight loss. CT shows multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules up to 2 cm and two lytic lesions in the pelvis; biopsy of a lung nodule confirms metastatic clear cell carcinoma. She is fully active, and her blood counts, calcium and liver tests are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line systemic treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
For metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma, first-line treatment is an immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination: a PD-1 inhibitor with a VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (for example pembrolizumab with axitinib or lenvatinib, or nivolumab with cabozantinib), or nivolumab with ipilimumab. These combinations improved survival over a tyrosine kinase inhibitor alone. Bone metastases may also need radiation for pain and a bone-protective agent.

Takeaway: metastatic clear cell RCC is treated first with checkpoint inhibitor-based combinations, not chemotherapy.

whyNot.A: Platinum chemotherapy is used for urothelial carcinoma; RCC is largely resistant to cytotoxic drugs.
whyNot.B: Sarcoma chemotherapy regimens have no role in clear cell RCC.
whyNot.D: Progestins were used historically with minimal benefit and are no longer recommended.
whyNot.E: Radiation can palliate individual symptomatic lesions but is not systemic therapy for widespread disease.

items.objective: Choose immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination therapy for metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because her father felt a hard lump on the right side of her abdomen while dressing her. She is otherwise well. Blood pressure is 112/72 mm Hg (above the 95th percentile for her age and height). Examination shows a smooth, firm, nontender mass in the right flank that does not cross the midline. Urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic study?

options.label: E
options.html: Urine homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid

items.explanationHtml:
A unilateral flank mass with hypertension and hematuria in a preschool child suggests Wilms tumour. Abdominal ultrasonography is the first study: it shows whether the mass is solid or cystic, whether it arises from the kidney or adrenal, and whether tumour extends into the renal vein or inferior vena cava. CT or MRI of the abdomen and chest CT follow for staging. Repeated palpation should be avoided because it can rupture the tumour.

Takeaway: abdominal mass in a young child: ultrasound first.

whyNot.B: Marrow aspiration stages neuroblastoma; Wilms tumour rarely involves marrow.
whyNot.C: Needle aspiration of a suspected Wilms tumour risks tumour spill and upstaging.
whyNot.D: Plain films add little; they may show calcification in neuroblastoma but cannot characterise the mass.
whyNot.E: Urine catecholamine metabolites help diagnose neuroblastoma, which usually crosses the midline; imaging should come first.

items.objective: Choose abdominal ultrasonography as the initial study for a suspected Wilms tumour.

items.stemHtml: A 4-month-old boy with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, confirmed by methylation testing at 11p15.5, is brought for a well-child visit. He had an omphalocele repaired at birth and neonatal hypoglycemia that has resolved. He is growing along the 95th percentile. Examination shows macroglossia and asymmetric enlargement of the right leg. Which of the following is the most appropriate surveillance for tumours?

options.label: A
options.html: Abdominal ultrasonography every 3 months and serum alpha-fetoprotein

options.label: B
options.html: Chest radiography once a year until 10 years of age

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the brain once a year until 5 years of age

options.label: D
options.html: No surveillance unless a mass is felt on examination

options.label: E
options.html: Urine catecholamine metabolites every 6 months until age 10

items.explanationHtml:
Children with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome have a raised risk of embryonal tumours in early childhood, mainly Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma. Surveillance with abdominal ultrasonography every 3 months until about 7 years finds Wilms tumours at a lower stage, and alpha-fetoprotein is measured regularly in the first years of life to detect hepatoblastoma.

Takeaway: Beckwith-Wiedemann: ultrasound every 3 months until about 7, plus AFP in early childhood.

whyNot.B: Chest radiographs do not detect the abdominal embryonal tumours this syndrome predisposes to.
whyNot.C: Brain tumours are not a characteristic risk in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
whyNot.D: Waiting for a palpable mass leads to later-stage diagnosis; structured surveillance is recommended.
whyNot.E: Neuroblastoma is not the main tumour risk in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

items.objective: Arrange abdominal ultrasound and AFP surveillance in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with painless gross hematuria has cystoscopy and transurethral resection of a 4-cm bladder tumour. Pathology shows high-grade urothelial carcinoma invading the detrusor (muscularis propria). CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. His creatinine clearance is 78 mL/min, hearing is normal and he is fully active. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy followed by radical cystectomy

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat transurethral resection and surveillance cystoscopy

items.explanationHtml:
Tumour invading the muscularis propria is muscle-invasive bladder cancer (at least T2). For localised disease in a patient fit for cisplatin, neoadjuvant cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy followed by radical cystectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection improves survival over surgery alone. Bladder-sparing trimodality therapy is an alternative for selected patients.

Takeaway: muscle-invasive bladder cancer: neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy, then radical cystectomy.

whyNot.A: BCG treats non-muscle-invasive disease and cannot control a tumour that has invaded the detrusor.
whyNot.C: Partial cystectomy is suitable only for rare, solitary tumours in favourable sites, and omitting neoadjuvant chemotherapy loses its survival benefit.
whyNot.D: Surveillance after resection is inadequate once the tumour has invaded muscle.
whyNot.E: Checkpoint inhibitors alone are for metastatic or cisplatin-ineligible settings, not first-line curative treatment here.

items.objective: Treat localised muscle-invasive bladder cancer with neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy and radical cystectomy.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man has dark brown urine and puffy eyelids 2 weeks after a sore throat. Blood pressure is 148/94 mm Hg. Phase-contrast microscopy of fresh urine shows many red cells; most are irregular in size and have blebs projecting from a ring-shaped membrane. Which of the following best explains the abnormal shape of these red cells?

options.label: A
options.html: Contraction of the cells in hypertonic medullary interstitium after diapedesis through peritubular capillaries

options.label: B
options.html: Damage during passage through the glomerular basement membrane and then the changing tubular fluid

options.label: C
options.html: Lysis by antibodies and complement in the renal pelvis before entry into the ureter

options.label: D
options.html: Mechanical shearing by fibrin strands in small renal arterioles of the cortex

options.label: E
options.html: Spherocyte formation in the spleen before the cells are filtered by the kidney

items.explanationHtml:
Dysmorphic red cells, especially acanthocytes (ring forms with blebs), are the signature of glomerular bleeding. Cells squeeze through gaps in an inflamed glomerular basement membrane and are then exposed to large swings in osmolality and pH along the tubule. Here the cause is postinfectious glomerulonephritis.

Takeaway: dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts place hematuria in the glomerulus.

whyNot.A: Red cells do not enter urine across peritubular capillaries; this mechanism is not how glomerular dysmorphism arises.
whyNot.C: Antibody-mediated lysis in the collecting system is not a mechanism of hematuria; lysed cells would not appear as acanthocytes.
whyNot.D: Shearing by fibrin in arterioles produces schistocytes in blood in thrombotic microangiopathy; it does not explain urinary acanthocytes.
whyNot.E: Intact red cells are not filtered by a normal glomerulus, and spherocytes are smooth spheres without blebs.

items.objective: Explain why glomerular hematuria produces dysmorphic red cells.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman is found on her kitchen floor, where she had lain for about 2 days after a fall. Her urine is reddish brown. The urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows 0–2 red cells per high-power field. Her plasma is straw coloured. Which of the following serum findings is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
A heme-positive dipstick with almost no red cells means a pigment: hemoglobin or myoglobin. Prolonged immobility after a fall causes pressure necrosis of muscle (rhabdomyolysis). Myoglobin is small and is filtered and cleared quickly, so the plasma stays clear, unlike hemoglobinemia, which turns plasma pink. The serum creatine kinase is very high.

Takeaway: heme-positive urine without red cells plus clear plasma means myoglobinuria; check creatine kinase.

whyNot.A: Low haptoglobin marks intravascular hemolysis, in which free hemoglobin makes the plasma pink.
whyNot.C: Conjugated bilirubin darkens urine but does not react on the blood pad.
whyNot.D: A raised reticulocyte count reflects marrow response to anemia or hemolysis, not muscle injury.
whyNot.E: Unconjugated bilirubin rises with hemolysis but is albumin bound and never reaches the urine.

items.objective: Distinguish myoglobinuria from hematuria and hemoglobinuria using the dipstick, microscopy and plasma colour.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man has fatigue, back pain and constipation. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL, serum calcium 11.8 mg/dL and serum creatinine 2.3 mg/dL. Urine dipstick shows trace protein. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 3.1 g/g. Which of the following best explains the mismatch between the dipstick and the protein-to-creatinine ratio?

options.label: A
options.html: The dipstick reacts mainly with albumin, and the excreted protein is mostly immunoglobulin light chains

options.label: B
options.html: The dipstick reacts mainly with light chains, and the excreted protein is mostly albumin

options.label: C
options.html: High urine calcium inactivates the indicator dye on the protein pad

options.label: D
options.html: Low urine creatinine from loss of muscle mass falsely raises the ratio

options.label: E
options.html: Tamm-Horsfall protein in the sample is falsely measured as albumin

items.explanationHtml:
The dipstick protein pad relies on albumin's negative charge and detects other proteins poorly. In multiple myeloma (anemia, hypercalcemia, renal failure, bone pain) the kidney filters large amounts of free light chains (overflow proteinuria, Bence Jones protein), which the dipstick misses but the total protein measurement detects. Urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains confirm it.

Takeaway: trace dipstick protein with a high total protein ratio means non-albumin protein, classically light chains.

whyNot.B: This reverses the problem: the dipstick is insensitive to light chains, not to albumin.
whyNot.C: Calcium does not inactivate the protein pad; the mismatch is about which protein is present.
whyNot.D: Low creatinine excretion can inflate a ratio somewhat, but not enough to explain 3 g/g with a trace dipstick in a man with features of myeloma.
whyNot.E: Tamm-Horsfall protein is a normal, small part of urinary protein and does not explain grams per day.

items.objective: Recognise overflow proteinuria from light chains as a cause of dipstick-negative proteinuria.

items.stemHtml: A 21-year-old Black man who is a college athlete has had two episodes of painless gross hematuria after training in hot weather. He has no flank pain. His hemoglobin concentration and blood smear are normal. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows HbA 58% and HbS 40%. Urine osmolality after overnight water restriction is 320 mOsm/kg (serum 290 mOsm/kg). Which of the following best explains both the hematuria and the urine concentrating defect?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibody deposition along the glomerular basement membrane

options.label: B
options.html: Calcium phosphate deposition in the cortical collecting ducts

options.label: C
options.html: Sickling in the hypertonic, hypoxic renal medulla with damage to the vasa recta and papillae

options.label: D
options.html: Thinning of the glomerular basement membrane from a type IV collagen variant

options.label: E
options.html: Urate crystal deposition in the medullary interstitium

items.explanationHtml:
Even in sickle cell trait red cells sickle in the renal medulla, where oxygen tension is low and osmolality and acidity are high. Sickling blocks the vasa recta, which causes microinfarcts of the papillae (hematuria, sometimes papillary necrosis) and disrupts the countercurrent system, so the kidney cannot concentrate urine well (hyposthenuria). Hematuria is often worse with dehydration and exertion.

Takeaway: sickle cell trait can cause painless hematuria and a concentrating defect through medullary sickling.

whyNot.A: Anti-GBM disease causes rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with dysmorphic red cells, not exertion-linked painless hematuria with normal function.
whyNot.B: Nephrocalcinosis can impair concentration but is not linked to his hemoglobin trait and rarely causes episodic gross hematuria.
whyNot.D: Thin basement membrane disease causes persistent microscopic glomerular hematuria; it does not impair concentrating ability.
whyNot.E: Chronic urate nephropathy is a disease of gout and lead exposure, not of a young athlete with sickle trait.

items.objective: Explain how sickle cell trait causes hematuria and impaired urine concentration.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man has worked for 20 years in a battery factory with cadmium exposure. Serum creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL and serum glucose 88 mg/dL. Urine dipstick shows trace protein and 1+ glucose. A 24-hour urine collection contains 1.2 g of protein, and electrophoresis shows that most of it migrates as small proteins, with a large beta-2 microglobulin band and little albumin. Which part of the nephron is most likely damaged?

options.label: E
options.html: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

items.explanationHtml:
Small proteins such as beta-2 microglobulin are filtered freely and normally almost fully reabsorbed by endocytosis in the proximal tubule. When that segment is injured (cadmium, other heavy metals, Fanconi syndrome, some drugs), these proteins appear in urine as tubular proteinuria, which is mostly not albumin and so reads weakly on the dipstick. Glucosuria with normal plasma glucose is another sign of proximal dysfunction.

Takeaway: low-molecular-weight proteinuria (beta-2 microglobulin) plus normoglycemic glucosuria points to proximal tubule injury.

whyNot.A: Principal cells handle sodium, potassium and water; injury there does not cause loss of small filtered proteins or glucose.
whyNot.B: The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs sodium chloride and calcium, not filtered proteins or glucose.
whyNot.C: Podocyte injury causes albumin-dominant (glomerular) proteinuria.
whyNot.E: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs sodium, potassium and chloride and secretes Tamm-Horsfall protein; it does not reclaim filtered small proteins.

items.objective: Recognise tubular proteinuria from proximal tubule injury.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy has had swelling around his eyes and ankles for 10 days. Blood pressure is normal. Serum albumin is 1.9 g/dL and cholesterol 380 mg/dL. Urine microscopy shows round bodies that, under polarised light, show a Maltese-cross pattern. Which of the following do these structures most likely represent?

options.label: B
options.html: Cholesterol-laden tubular cells and lipid droplets

items.explanationHtml:
In nephrotic syndrome, lipoproteins leak through the glomerulus and are taken up by tubular cells, which slough as oval fat bodies; free cholesterol esters show a Maltese cross under polarised light. Lipiduria and fatty casts accompany heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia.

Takeaway: Maltese-cross lipid bodies in urine mean lipiduria of nephrotic syndrome.

whyNot.A: Calcium oxalate crystals look like envelopes or dumbbells and are not related to hypoalbuminemia.
whyNot.C: Cystine forms flat hexagons, seen in cystinuria with stones.
whyNot.D: Neutrophils appear as granular cells with lobed nuclei and suggest infection or inflammation, not lipiduria.
whyNot.E: Yeast are budding ovoid forms and do not show a Maltese cross.

items.objective: Identify oval fat bodies with a Maltese cross as a sign of nephrotic syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man has had stiff, painful knees and hips for several years, and the cartilage of his ears has a blue-black tinge. He reports that his urine turns dark, almost black, if left standing in a container. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive defect of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase in tyrosine breakdown. Homogentisic acid accumulates and is excreted; in urine it oxidises and polymerises to a dark pigment when exposed to air, especially in alkaline urine. Deposition in connective tissue (ochronosis) darkens cartilage and causes early degenerative arthritis of large joints and the spine.

Takeaway: urine that blackens on standing plus dark cartilage and early arthritis is alkaptonuria.

whyNot.A: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency causes homocystinuria: lens dislocation, thrombosis and a marfanoid habitus.
whyNot.B: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency is tyrosinemia type I, with liver failure and renal Fanconi syndrome in infancy.
whyNot.D: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency is phenylketonuria, with a musty odour and intellectual disability if untreated.
whyNot.E: Tyrosinase deficiency causes oculocutaneous albinism, with reduced, not increased, pigment.

items.objective: Link urine that darkens on standing to alkaptonuria and its enzyme defect.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man is admitted with septic shock from a perforated diverticulum and receives vasopressors for 2 days. His urine output falls to 300 mL/day, and serum creatinine rises from 1.0 to 3.4 mg/dL over 3 days. Which of the following urine sediment findings is most likely?

options.label: C
options.html: Muddy brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells

options.label: D
options.html: Oval fat bodies with fatty casts

options.label: E
options.html: Red blood cell casts with dysmorphic red cells

items.explanationHtml:
Prolonged hypotension causes ischemic acute tubular necrosis. Injured tubular cells slough into the lumen and break down, forming coarse muddy brown granular casts, along with free renal tubular epithelial cells. The straight portion of the proximal tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb are most vulnerable because of their high oxygen demand in a low-oxygen region.

Takeaway: muddy brown granular casts mean acute tubular necrosis.

whyNot.A: Broad waxy casts form in dilated, atrophic tubules and indicate advanced chronic kidney disease.
whyNot.B: Hyaline casts alone are typical of prerenal states, not established tubular injury after days of shock.
whyNot.D: Oval fat bodies and fatty casts indicate the lipiduria of nephrotic syndrome.
whyNot.E: Red cell casts mean glomerulonephritis, not ischemic tubular injury.

items.objective: Match muddy brown granular casts to acute tubular necrosis.

items.stemHtml:
A 49-year-old man has passed about 5 L of urine a day for 2 weeks, with thirst and a 4-kg weight loss. Laboratory studies show:

TestResult
Serum sodium141 mEq/L
Serum glucose452 mg/dL
Serum osmolality306 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality390 mOsm/kg
Urine glucose4+

Which of the following best describes the mechanism of his polyuria?

options.label: A
options.html: Failure of the collecting duct to respond to antidiuretic hormone

options.label: B
options.html: Impaired release of antidiuretic hormone from the posterior pituitary

options.label: C
options.html: Osmotic diuresis from filtered glucose exceeding proximal tubular reabsorption

options.label: D
options.html: Primary excess water intake that suppresses antidiuretic hormone

options.label: E
options.html: Washout of the medullary gradient by a loop diuretic effect of hyperglycemia

items.explanationHtml:
Glucose filtered above the transport maximum of proximal SGLT2 and SGLT1 stays in the tubule and holds water with it: an osmotic (solute) diuresis. The urine osmolality is near or above plasma (here 390 mOsm/kg), which separates a solute diuresis from a water diuresis, where the urine is dilute (well below plasma osmolality).

Takeaway: polyuria with urine osmolality at or above plasma is a solute diuresis; with very dilute urine it is a water diuresis.

whyNot.A: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus produces dilute urine, far below plasma osmolality.
whyNot.B: Central diabetes insipidus also produces dilute urine, not urine more concentrated than plasma.
whyNot.D: Primary polydipsia produces very dilute urine and a low-normal serum sodium.
whyNot.E: Hyperglycemia has no loop-diuretic action on the thick ascending limb; the solute load explains the diuresis.

items.objective: Use urine osmolality to separate a solute diuresis from a water diuresis.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man has microscopic hematuria found during an insurance examination. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. He has no dysuria, flank pain or recent exercise, and he takes no medications. Blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Repeat urinalysis 2 weeks later shows 30 red blood cells per high-power field with normal morphology, no casts, no protein and no leukocyte esterase or nitrite. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
He has confirmed nonglomerular microscopic hematuria and is at high risk of urothelial cancer (age above 60, more than 30 pack-years, more than 25 red cells per field). High-risk patients need evaluation of both the bladder and the upper tracts: cystoscopy plus CT urography.

Takeaway: high-risk microscopic hematuria (older, heavy smoker, many red cells) needs cystoscopy and CT urography.

whyNot.B: PSA screens for prostate cancer and does not evaluate the bladder or upper tract for the source of hematuria.
whyNot.C: Ultrasonography alone misses small urothelial tumours of the bladder and upper tract and omits the bladder examination.
whyNot.D: Repeat testing alone is reserved for some low-risk patients; delay is inappropriate at his risk level.
whyNot.E: Cytology is insensitive for low-grade tumours and does not replace cystoscopy and imaging.

items.objective: Evaluate high-risk microscopic hematuria with cystoscopy and CT urography.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman comes for a routine examination. She feels well. A urine dipstick done in the office is 1+ for blood and negative for protein, leukocyte esterase and nitrite. Her last menstrual period ended 12 days ago. She has never smoked. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Microscopic examination of a urine specimen

items.explanationHtml:
A positive dipstick for blood is not hematuria until microscopy confirms red cells (3 or more per high-power field). The blood pad also reacts to free hemoglobin and myoglobin, and dipsticks give false positives. Further evaluation, if any, depends on the microscopy result and her risk group.

Takeaway: confirm a heme-positive dipstick with urine microscopy before any hematuria work-up.

whyNot.A: Cystoscopy is not done for an unconfirmed dipstick result in a low-risk young woman.
whyNot.B: Imaging is premature before hematuria is confirmed and the risk group is known.
whyNot.D: There are no features of glomerular disease (no protein, normal blood pressure).
whyNot.E: Without pyuria, nitrite or symptoms, infection is unlikely, and culture does not confirm hematuria.

items.objective: Confirm dipstick-positive blood with microscopy before evaluating hematuria.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man is evaluated on the second day after hip fracture repair because he has passed only 90 mL of urine in the past 8 hours. He is restless and has lower abdominal discomfort. He has benign prostatic hyperplasia and received oxybutynin for bladder spasms and intravenous morphine for pain. Blood pressure is 142/84 mm Hg and pulse 92/min. The lower abdomen is dull to percussion above the pubis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Bladder ultrasonography followed by urethral catheterisation

options.label: E
options.html: Urine sodium and creatinine to calculate the fractional excretion of sodium

items.explanationHtml:
New oliguria in an older man with prostatic enlargement who has received an anticholinergic and an opioid, with suprapubic dullness and discomfort, is acute urinary retention until proven otherwise. A bladder scan confirms a large residual volume, and a urethral catheter relieves the obstruction and restores urine flow. Lower-tract obstruction should be excluded before fluid or diuretic decisions.

Takeaway: in sudden oliguria, check the bladder first.

whyNot.B: A diuretic cannot work against bladder outlet obstruction and could worsen discomfort and volume status.
whyNot.C: He shows no signs of hypovolemia, and fluid will not drain an obstructed bladder.
whyNot.D: Renal imaging may follow if upper-tract obstruction is suspected after the bladder is drained, but it is not the first step.
whyNot.E: Urine indices are uninterpretable until obstruction is excluded and urine can be collected.

items.objective: Exclude and relieve bladder outlet obstruction first in acute oliguria.

items.stemHtml:
A 26-year-old man of Mediterranean ancestry has dark urine and fatigue 2 days after starting a sulfonamide-containing antibiotic. He is pale and mildly jaundiced. Laboratory studies show:

TestResult
Hemoglobin8.9 g/dL
Reticulocytes6% of red cells
Lactate dehydrogenase820 U/L (N = 45–200 U/L)
Haptoglobinbelow 10 mg/dL (N = 30–200 mg/dL)
Bilirubin, total3.2 mg/dL
Bilirubin, direct0.3 mg/dL
Creatine kinase110 U/L (N = 25–200 U/L)
Urine dipstickblood 3+
Urine microscopy0–1 red cells per high-power field

Plasma is pink after centrifugation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his dark urine?
items.explanationHtml:
A heme-positive dipstick with no red cells, pink plasma, low haptoglobin, high LDH, raised unconjugated bilirubin and reticulocytosis after an oxidant drug is intravascular hemolysis (most likely G6PD deficiency), with free hemoglobin filtered into the urine. Stop the drug, support with fluids, and test G6PD activity after recovery (levels can be falsely normal during the episode because young cells have more enzyme).

Takeaway: heme-positive urine without red cells plus pink plasma and low haptoglobin is hemoglobinuria.

whyNot.A: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin is normal, so bilirubinuria is not the cause; bilirubin also does not react on the blood pad.
whyNot.B: Glomerular hematuria would show many dysmorphic red cells on microscopy.
whyNot.D: Normal creatine kinase and pink plasma rule against myoglobinuria.
whyNot.E: Porphyrins do not react on the blood pad, and the hemolysis profile is not explained by porphyria.

items.objective: Identify hemoglobinuria from intravascular hemolysis using a chart of hemolysis markers and urine findings.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy has a sports physical. He feels well and has no edema. Blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg. A random urine dipstick in the afternoon shows 2+ protein and no blood; microscopy is normal. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Measure protein in a first-morning urine sample

options.label: D
options.html: Serum complement and antinuclear antibody testing

items.explanationHtml:
Isolated low-grade proteinuria in a healthy adolescent with normal blood pressure, sediment and creatinine is most often orthostatic or transient. A first-morning sample (or a split upright and recumbent collection) tests this: protein that disappears overnight is orthostatic and benign.

Takeaway: in a healthy teenager with isolated proteinuria, check a first-morning urine before any work-up.

whyNot.A: Biopsy is for persistent, significant proteinuria or other signs of kidney disease, not a first finding.
whyNot.C: Imaging is not useful for isolated proteinuria at this stage.
whyNot.D: Serologic testing is for persistent proteinuria with features of glomerulonephritis or systemic disease.
whyNot.E: Treatment is not indicated until persistent pathologic proteinuria is confirmed.

items.objective: Test for orthostatic proteinuria with a first-morning sample in a healthy adolescent.

items.stemHtml: The first-morning urine sample shows a protein-to-creatinine ratio of 0.08 g/g. A urine sample collected at the end of a school day shows 0.6 g/g. Microscopy remains normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Kidney biopsy to exclude early glomerular disease

options.label: B
options.html: A low-protein diet with repeat testing in 3 months

options.label: D
options.html: Reassurance with a periodic urine and blood pressure recheck

options.label: E
options.html: Restriction of sports until the proteinuria resolves

items.explanationHtml:
Normal protein after recumbency and modest protein after hours upright is orthostatic proteinuria. Long-term follow-up shows an excellent prognosis, so management is reassurance with a periodic recheck of urine and blood pressure. He can play sports.

Takeaway: orthostatic proteinuria is benign: reassure and recheck periodically.

whyNot.A: Biopsy is not indicated for benign orthostatic proteinuria.
whyNot.B: Diet changes have no role in a benign postural finding.
whyNot.C: There is no glomerular disease to treat.
whyNot.E: Exercise is safe; restriction would harm him without benefit.

items.objective: Reassure a patient with confirmed orthostatic proteinuria.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man is admitted with 3 days of vomiting. Blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg lying and 82/54 mm Hg sitting. His glomerular filtration rate is partly preserved by angiotensin II acting on the glomerular efferent arteriole. Compared with his state before the illness, which of the following best describes the effect of this efferent arteriolar constriction on renal plasma flow (RPF), GFR and filtration fraction (FF)?

options.label: A
options.html: RPF decreased, GFR decreased, FF unchanged

options.label: B
options.html: RPF decreased, GFR increased, FF increased

options.label: C
options.html: RPF increased, GFR decreased, FF decreased

options.label: D
options.html: RPF increased, GFR increased, FF unchanged

options.label: E
options.html: RPF unchanged, GFR decreased, FF decreased

items.explanationHtml:
Constricting the efferent arteriole raises resistance downstream of the glomerulus, so less plasma flows through (RPF falls) but glomerular capillary pressure rises, which supports or raises GFR. With GFR up and RPF down, the filtration fraction rises. This is how angiotensin II defends GFR in volume depletion, and why blocking it with an ACE inhibitor can precipitate AKI.

Takeaway: efferent constriction lowers RPF, raises GFR and raises the filtration fraction.

whyNot.A: Equal falls in RPF and GFR with an unchanged FF describe afferent constriction, as with NSAIDs.
whyNot.C: Rising RPF with falling GFR and FF is efferent dilation, the effect of ACE inhibitors and ARBs.
whyNot.D: Rising RPF and GFR with an unchanged FF is afferent dilation, as with prostaglandins.
whyNot.E: Falling GFR and FF with unchanged RPF follows raised Bowman space pressure (obstruction) or raised plasma oncotic pressure.

items.objective: Predict the effects of efferent arteriolar constriction on renal plasma flow, GFR and filtration fraction.

items.stemHtml:
A 45-year-old woman collects a 24-hour urine sample to estimate her kidney function. A blood sample is drawn during the collection.

MeasurementValue
24-hour urine volume1,440 mL
Urine creatinine120 mg/dL
Serum creatinine1.5 mg/dL (N = 0.6–1.2)

Which of the following is closest to her creatinine clearance?
items.explanationHtml:
Clearance = (U × V) / P. Urine flow is 1,440 mL over 1,440 minutes, or 1 mL/min. Clearance = (120 mg/dL × 1 mL/min) / 1.5 mg/dL = 80 mL/min. Because creatinine is also secreted a little by the proximal tubule, this slightly overestimates the true GFR.

Takeaway: clearance = UV/P; convert urine volume to mL/min first.

whyNot.A: This is half the correct value, as if urine flow were taken as 0.5 mL/min.
whyNot.B: This does not follow from the numbers; it would need a urine creatinine of 90 mg/dL.
whyNot.D: This would need a urine creatinine of 180 mg/dL or a serum creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL.
whyNot.E: This would follow from dividing urine creatinine by a serum value of about 0.67 mg/dL, not 1.5.

items.objective: Calculate creatinine clearance from a timed urine collection.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old man has headache and blurred vision. Blood pressure is 238/142 mm Hg. Funduscopy shows retinal hemorrhages and papilledema. Serum creatinine is 3.4 mg/dL, up from 1.0 mg/dL a year ago. Urinalysis shows protein and red blood cells. The peripheral smear shows schistocytes. A kidney biopsy is performed. Which of the following arteriolar findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Amyloid deposits that show apple-green birefringence

options.label: B
options.html: Concentric smooth muscle layering with fibrinoid necrosis

options.label: D
options.html: Homogeneous pink hyaline thickening of the wall

options.label: E
options.html: Leukocytoclastic necrosis with immune complex deposits

items.explanationHtml:
Severe hypertension with papilledema, AKI and microangiopathic hemolysis is a hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension). Arterioles show hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, concentric ("onion-skin") layers of smooth muscle cells and reduplicated basement membrane, often with fibrinoid necrosis. The kidney surface has pinpoint cortical hemorrhages.

Takeaway: onion-skin hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis and fibrinoid necrosis mark malignant hypertension; hyaline arteriolosclerosis marks long-standing benign hypertension and diabetes.

whyNot.A: Amyloid deposits occur in AL or AA amyloidosis, which causes nephrotic-range proteinuria rather than a hypertensive crisis.
whyNot.C: Granulomatous vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, giant cell arteritis) does not explain the papilledema with this pressure.
whyNot.D: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is the slow lesion of chronic, milder hypertension and diabetes.
whyNot.E: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis affects small vessels in immune complex disease, not this hypertensive picture.

items.objective: Identify hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis as the renal lesion of malignant hypertension.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy has blood pressure of 168/104 mm Hg on three visits. His father and paternal aunt developed hypertension as teenagers. Serum potassium is 3.0 mEq/L and bicarbonate 31 mEq/L. Plasma renin activity and aldosterone are both low. Blood pressure does not improve with spironolactone but falls with amiloride. Which of the following best describes the underlying defect?

options.label: A
options.html: Excess cortisol acting on mineralocorticoid receptors

options.label: B
options.html: Gain of function of the epithelial sodium channel

options.label: C
options.html: Loss of function of the Na⁺-Cl⁻ cotransporter

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of function of the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter

options.label: E
options.html: Overproduction of aldosterone by an adrenal adenoma

items.explanationHtml:
Early, autosomal dominant hypertension with hypokalemic alkalosis, low renin and low aldosterone and a response to an ENaC blocker but not to spironolactone is Liddle syndrome. Mutations stop ENaC from being removed from the principal-cell membrane, so sodium is reabsorbed without aldosterone. Amiloride or triamterene blocks the channel directly.

Takeaway: hypertension, hypokalemia and suppressed renin and aldosterone that respond to amiloride is Liddle syndrome.

whyNot.A: Apparent mineralocorticoid excess also gives low renin and aldosterone, but it responds to spironolactone, which blocks the receptor that cortisol is stimulating.
whyNot.C: Loss of NCC is Gitelman syndrome, which causes low or normal blood pressure and high renin.
whyNot.D: Loss of NKCC2 is Bartter syndrome, with low or normal blood pressure and high renin and aldosterone.
whyNot.E: Primary aldosteronism has high aldosterone and responds to spironolactone.

items.objective: Recognise Liddle syndrome as ENaC gain of function with suppressed renin and aldosterone.

items.stemHtml:
A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 18 years and stable CKD (eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73 m²) has routine laboratory studies. He takes metformin and amlodipine and no potassium supplements.

SerumValue
Sodium138 mEq/L
Potassium5.9 mEq/L
Chloride112 mEq/L
Bicarbonate18 mEq/L
Glucose142 mg/dL

Urine pH is 5.2. Plasma renin activity and aldosterone are low. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the acid-base disorder?

options.label: B
options.html: Impaired distal hydrogen ion secretion by intercalated cells

options.label: C
options.html: Impaired renal ammonium excretion from low aldosterone effect

items.explanationHtml:
The anion gap is 138 − (112 + 18) = 8, a normal anion gap acidosis with hyperkalemia and an acidic urine. This is type 4 RTA from hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, common in diabetic kidney disease. Low aldosterone reduces potassium secretion; the resulting hyperkalemia suppresses proximal ammoniagenesis, so the kidney cannot excrete enough acid as ammonium even though it can still lower urine pH.

Takeaway: hyperkalemic normal anion gap acidosis with urine pH below 5.5 in diabetes is type 4 RTA.

whyNot.A: Type 2 RTA causes hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.
whyNot.B: Type 1 RTA causes hypokalemia and a urine pH that stays above 5.5.
whyNot.D: Diabetic ketoacidosis causes a high anion gap acidosis with marked hyperglycemia.
whyNot.E: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis causes a high anion gap and usually occurs in acute illness.

items.objective: Diagnose type 4 RTA from a hyperkalemic normal anion gap acidosis in diabetic kidney disease.

items.stemHtml:
A 51-year-old man with HIV infection has had bone pain in his hips and feet for 4 months. He has taken a tenofovir disoproxil fumarate-containing regimen for 6 years. Laboratory studies:

TestValue
Serum glucose88 mg/dL
Serum phosphorus1.8 mg/dL
Serum uric acid1.9 mg/dL
Serum bicarbonate18 mEq/L
Serum potassium3.2 mEq/L
Urine dipstickGlucose 2+, protein 1+

Which part of the nephron is most likely affected?

options.label: E
options.html: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

items.explanationHtml:
Glucose in the urine with a normal blood glucose, low phosphate (causing osteomalacia and bone pain), low uric acid, hypokalemia and a normal anion gap acidosis add up to Fanconi syndrome: generalised failure of proximal tubule reabsorption. Tenofovir disoproxil accumulates in proximal tubular cells and injures their mitochondria.

Takeaway: glycosuria with normal blood glucose plus phosphate and bicarbonate wasting points to the proximal tubule (Fanconi syndrome).

whyNot.A: Principal-cell disorders change sodium, potassium and water handling but do not waste glucose, phosphate or urate.
whyNot.B: Distal convoluted tubule defects (as in Gitelman syndrome) waste sodium chloride and magnesium, not glucose.
whyNot.C: Podocyte injury causes heavy albuminuria and edema, not glycosuria with phosphate wasting.
whyNot.E: Thick ascending limb defects (as in Bartter syndrome) cause hypokalemic alkalosis, not acidosis with glycosuria.

items.objective: Localise Fanconi syndrome to the proximal tubule and recognise tenofovir as a cause.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old girl has her third episode of right flank pain and hematuria since age 9. Her older brother has also had kidney stones. Urine microscopy shows flat, six-sided crystals, and a urine cyanide-nitroprusside test is positive. A defect in which of the following is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Apical transporter for dibasic amino acids in the proximal tubule

options.label: E
options.html: Vacuolar H⁺-ATPase of the α-intercalated cell

items.explanationHtml:
Hexagonal crystals and a positive cyanide-nitroprusside test mean cystine stones, from autosomal recessive cystinuria. The defect is in the apical transporter that reabsorbs cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine from the proximal tubule (and gut). Only cystine is insoluble enough to form stones. Treatment is high fluid intake, urine alkalinisation and, if needed, tiopronin.

Takeaway: hexagonal crystals = cystine = defective proximal reabsorption of dibasic amino acids.

whyNot.B: Alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase deficiency is primary hyperoxaluria type 1, which forms calcium oxalate stones and nephrocalcinosis.
whyNot.C: A defective lysosomal cystine transporter (cystinosin) causes cystinosis, with cystine crystals in tissues and Fanconi syndrome, not cystine stones.
whyNot.D: HGPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan syndrome) causes uric acid overproduction and uric acid stones, with neurologic features.
whyNot.E: Loss of the H⁺-ATPase causes distal (type 1) RTA with calcium phosphate stones.

items.objective: Identify cystinuria from hexagonal crystals and explain its transporter defect.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman had 90 cm of terminal ileum resected for Crohn disease 3 years ago. She has chronic loose, fatty stools and has now passed two radiopaque kidney stones. A 24-hour urine shows a high oxalate level with normal calcium. Which of the following is the main reason for her stones?

options.label: A
options.html: Excess hepatic synthesis of oxalate from glyoxylate

options.label: B
options.html: Free oxalate absorbed in the colon because fatty acids bind luminal calcium

options.label: C
options.html: Hypercalciuria from increased intestinal calcium absorption

options.label: D
options.html: Persistently alkaline urine from bicarbonate loss in stool

options.label: E
options.html: Urease-producing bacteria colonising the urinary tract

items.explanationHtml:
After ileal resection, bile acids are lost and fat is malabsorbed. In the gut lumen, unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium, so dietary oxalate that would normally leave the body as insoluble calcium oxalate stays free and is absorbed by the colon (bile acids reaching the colon also make it more permeable). Urine oxalate rises, and calcium oxalate stones form; diarrhea adds dehydration and low urine citrate. Treatment includes a low-fat, low-oxalate diet and calcium taken with meals.

Takeaway: fat malabsorption causes enteric hyperoxaluria and calcium oxalate stones.

whyNot.A: Hepatic overproduction of oxalate is primary hyperoxaluria, a genetic disorder that typically presents in childhood.
whyNot.C: Her urine calcium is normal; malabsorption tends to lower calcium absorption, not raise it.
whyNot.D: Diarrhea causes loss of bicarbonate and an acidic, low-volume urine, which favours uric acid stones, not alkaline urine.
whyNot.E: Urease-producing organisms cause struvite stones, not hyperoxaluria.

items.objective: Explain enteric hyperoxaluria as the cause of calcium oxalate stones after ileal resection.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man has cardiac arrest during surgery and is resuscitated after 25 minutes of low blood pressure. Over the next 2 days his urine output falls to 300 mL/day, and serum creatinine rises from 1.0 to 4.2 mg/dL. Urine microscopy shows many muddy brown granular casts. Which of the following nephron segments is most susceptible to the injury causing these findings?

options.label: D
options.html: Straight segment of the proximal tubule

options.label: E
options.html: Thin descending limb of the loop of Henle

items.explanationHtml:
Oliguric AKI with muddy brown granular casts after a period of shock is ischemic acute tubular necrosis. The straight segment of the proximal tubule in the outer medulla, together with the medullary thick ascending limb, is most vulnerable, because these cells have high energy demands for active transport and lie where oxygen delivery is lowest.

Takeaway: ischemic ATN hits the proximal straight tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb first.

whyNot.A: The parietal epithelium of Bowman capsule proliferates in crescentic glomerulonephritis, not in ischemic injury.
whyNot.B: Glomerular endothelial injury occurs in thrombotic microangiopathies and preeclampsia, not as the main lesion of ATN.
whyNot.C: Inner medullary collecting duct cells have relatively low energy needs and are less vulnerable to ischemia.
whyNot.E: The thin limbs transport passively and use little oxygen, so they tolerate ischemia well.

items.objective: Identify the nephron segments most vulnerable to ischemic acute tubular necrosis.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman has had CKD from diabetic nephropathy for 10 years; her eGFR is now 18 mL/min/1.73 m². She has bone pain. Which of the following sets of laboratory findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Calcium high, phosphate low, PTH high, calcitriol high

options.label: B
options.html: Calcium low, phosphate high, PTH high, calcitriol low

options.label: C
options.html: Calcium low, phosphate high, PTH low, calcitriol low

options.label: D
options.html: Calcium low, phosphate low, PTH high, calcitriol high

options.label: E
options.html: Calcium normal, phosphate normal, PTH low, calcitriol high

items.explanationHtml:
In advanced CKD, phosphate is retained, and both high FGF23 and loss of renal mass reduce 1α-hydroxylase, so calcitriol falls. Less calcitriol means less intestinal calcium absorption, and phosphate binds calcium, so calcium falls. Low calcium, high phosphate and low calcitriol all stimulate the parathyroids: secondary hyperparathyroidism with high PTH, which drives renal osteodystrophy.

Takeaway: CKD-MBD: low calcium, high phosphate, low calcitriol, high PTH and high FGF23.

whyNot.A: High calcium with low phosphate and high PTH is primary hyperparathyroidism with normal kidneys.
whyNot.C: Low calcium and high phosphate with a low PTH is hypoparathyroidism.
whyNot.D: Low calcium and phosphate with high PTH and high calcitriol is not a CKD pattern; low phosphate with high PTH suggests vitamin D deficiency with intact kidneys, in which calcitriol is not high.
whyNot.E: Normal minerals with low PTH and high calcitriol describe a granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis, with calcium usually high.

items.objective: Predict the mineral and hormone pattern of secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD.

items.stemHtml:
A 79-year-old woman has had 4 days of watery diarrhea after a viral illness in her care home. She feels dizzy on standing. She takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension, which was held yesterday. Blood pressure is 102/60 mm Hg lying and 84/50 mm Hg standing; pulse is 104/min. Mucous membranes are dry. Laboratory studies:

TestValue
Serum sodium141 mEq/L
Serum potassium3.4 mEq/L
Serum bicarbonate20 mEq/L
BUN58 mg/dL
Serum creatinine2.0 mg/dL (baseline 0.9)
Urine sodium11 mEq/L
Urine creatinine140 mg/dL
Urine microscopyFew hyaline casts; no cells

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Her FENa is (11 × 2.0) / (141 × 140) × 100 ≈ 0.1%, the BUN:creatinine ratio is 29, and the sediment is bland: a prerenal AKI from volume loss. The tubules are intact and holding on to sodium. Restore volume with isotonic crystalloid; creatinine should improve within 1–3 days. Keep the thiazide held.

Takeaway: FENa below 1%, BUN:creatinine above 20 and bland sediment in a volume-depleted patient: give isotonic fluids.

whyNot.A: A diuretic would deepen her volume depletion and worsen the AKI.
whyNot.C: Biopsy is for unexplained intrinsic disease (for example suspected glomerulonephritis), not for an obvious prerenal cause.
whyNot.D: Renal artery stenosis does not explain an AKI that followed diarrhea, and imaging would delay treatment.
whyNot.E: She has no refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, overload, poisoning or uremic complication.

items.objective: Recognise prerenal AKI from urine indices and treat it with isotonic fluid.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man is found on the floor of his apartment after an overdose of an opioid and a sedative; he may have lain there for about 20 hours. He is now alert. His left thigh is swollen and tender. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and pulse 102/min. Urine is dark brown; the dipstick is 3+ for blood, and microscopy shows 0–2 red blood cells per high-power field. Serum creatine kinase is 52,000 U/L, potassium 5.2 mEq/L and creatinine 1.6 mg/dL (baseline 0.9). Compartment pressures in the thigh are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Oral fluids and repeat creatine kinase in 48 hours

items.explanationHtml:
