Prolonged immobility, very high CK and a heme-positive dipstick with few red cells mean rhabdomyolysis with pigment-associated AKI. The key step is early, generous IV isotonic crystalloid, titrated to a high urine output while watching for overload, to dilute myoglobin and wash out casts. Monitor potassium, calcium, phosphate and the compartment.

Takeaway: rhabdomyolysis is treated with early, aggressive isotonic fluids.

whyNot.A: Early hypocalcemia in rhabdomyolysis is treated only if symptomatic or with dangerous hyperkalemia; giving calcium can deposit in injured muscle and cause rebound hypercalcemia later.
whyNot.B: Diuretics without volume repletion lower renal perfusion and do not prevent AKI.
whyNot.D: Oral fluids are too slow and too little for this degree of muscle injury.
whyNot.E: Dialysis is for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis or overload; none is present yet.

items.objective: Treat rhabdomyolysis with early, aggressive isotonic fluids.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with CKD G5 from hypertension, who has refused dialysis planning, has had 1 week of sharp chest pain that improves when he leans forward, plus nausea and itching. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), blood pressure 152/90 mm Hg and pulse 92/min, without pulsus paradoxus. A three-component friction rub is heard. BUN is 148 mg/dL, creatinine 11.2 mg/dL, potassium 5.3 mEq/L and bicarbonate 17 mEq/L. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation. Echocardiography shows a small effusion without tamponade. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Pericarditis in a patient with kidney failure and uremic symptoms is uremic pericarditis, a firm indication to start dialysis, which usually resolves it. Avoid anticoagulation with heparin during dialysis if possible, because of the risk of hemorrhagic effusion.

Takeaway: uremic pericarditis is an urgent indication for dialysis.

whyNot.A: NSAIDs and colchicine are standard for idiopathic or viral pericarditis but do not treat uremia, and NSAIDs harm residual kidney function.
whyNot.C: Bicarbonate corrects mild acidosis but does nothing for uremic pericarditis.
whyNot.D: Pericardiocentesis is for tamponade, which is absent.
whyNot.E: Steroids are not the treatment for uremic pericarditis.

items.objective: Recognise uremic pericarditis as an indication for dialysis.

items.stemHtml:
A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and CKD has a follow-up visit. She takes lisinopril 40 mg daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily and atorvastatin. She has no heart failure. Blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. Results of tests on two occasions 3 months apart are similar:

TestValue
eGFR52 mL/min/1.73 m²
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio410 mg/g
Serum potassium4.4 mEq/L
Hemoglobin A1c6.9%

Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to further reduce her risk of kidney failure?
items.explanationHtml:
She has type 2 diabetes with CKD G3a A3 and persistent albuminuria despite a maximal ACE inhibitor and an SGLT2 inhibitor, with eGFR above 25 and normal potassium. Adding the nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid antagonist finerenone lowers the risk of kidney failure and cardiovascular events in this group. Recheck potassium about 4 weeks after starting.

Takeaway: type 2 diabetes with residual albuminuria on RAS blockade plus SGLT2 inhibitor, eGFR at least 25 and normal potassium: add finerenone.

whyNot.A: A direct renin inhibitor added to an ACE inhibitor is dual RAS blockade, which raises hyperkalemia and AKI without benefit.
whyNot.C: Combining an ARB with an ACE inhibitor is also dual blockade and is not recommended.
whyNot.D: Spironolactone lacks evidence for kidney outcomes in this setting and causes more hyperkalemia; finerenone is the agent with that evidence.
whyNot.E: KDIGO advises about 0.8 g/kg/day protein in CKD; very-low-protein diets risk malnutrition.

items.objective: Add finerenone for persistent albuminuria in type 2 diabetic CKD already on an ACE inhibitor and SGLT2 inhibitor.

items.stemHtml:
A 72-year-old man with CKD G4 (eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73 m²) from hypertensive nephrosclerosis has increasing fatigue. He has no bleeding. Colonoscopy 2 years ago was normal. Laboratory studies:

TestValue
Hemoglobin8.9 g/dL
MCV86 fL
Reticulocytes0.6% of red cells
Serum ferritin62 ng/mL (N = 15–200)
Transferrin saturation14% (N = 20–50)
Vitamin B12 and folateNormal

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Iron repletion, then reassess the hemoglobin

options.label: D
options.html: Start epoetin alfa to a hemoglobin target of 13 g/dL

items.explanationHtml:
Anemia of CKD is caused mainly by low erythropoietin, but iron deficiency (here transferrin saturation 14% with a ferritin below 100 ng/mL) is common and must be corrected first; it may raise hemoglobin by itself, and ESAs work poorly without iron. Give iron (often IV in CKD), then reassess. If hemoglobin stays below about 10 g/dL, an ESA can be started, aiming to avoid transfusions without normalising hemoglobin.

Takeaway: in anemia of CKD, replete iron before starting an ESA, and never target a normal hemoglobin.

whyNot.A: A marrow biopsy is not needed for a normocytic, hypoproliferative anemia with a clear explanation.
whyNot.C: Transfusion is for severe symptoms or instability; it also sensitises future transplant candidates.
whyNot.D: Targeting hemoglobin of 13 g/dL with an ESA raises stroke, thrombosis and mortality, and iron should be replaced first.
whyNot.E: Corticosteroids have no role in anemia of CKD.

items.objective: Correct iron deficiency before starting an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent in anemia of CKD.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 5 hours of colicky left flank pain radiating to the groin and nausea. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), and other vital signs are normal. Urinalysis shows red blood cells without leukocyte esterase, nitrite or bacteria. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Noncontrast CT shows a 6-mm stone in the distal left ureter with mild hydronephrosis. After intravenous ketorolac his pain is controlled, and he is tolerating oral fluids. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Oral tamsulosin, analgesia and urine straining, with follow-up

options.label: E
options.html: Potassium citrate to dissolve the stone

items.explanationHtml:
A distal ureteral stone of 5–10 mm without infection, AKI or uncontrolled pain can be managed with a trial of passage. An alpha blocker (tamsulosin) relaxes ureteral smooth muscle and improves passage; give an NSAID for pain, strain the urine to catch the stone for analysis, and arrange follow-up imaging. Refer for removal if the stone has not passed in about 4–6 weeks.

Takeaway: uncomplicated distal ureteral stone 5–10 mm: medical expulsive therapy with tamsulosin.

whyNot.A: There are no signs of infection; antibiotics are not needed.
whyNot.B: Emergency decompression is for infection with obstruction, AKI, a solitary kidney or intractable symptoms.
whyNot.D: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy is for large renal or staghorn stones, not a small distal ureteral stone.
whyNot.E: Alkalinisation can dissolve uric acid stones, but this stone is visible on CT without its composition known, and dissolution is not the first-line approach for a passable stone.

items.objective: Manage an uncomplicated 5–10 mm distal ureteral stone with medical expulsive therapy.

items.stemHtml:
A 45-year-old woman has had three calcium oxalate stones in 4 years. Serum calcium, PTH and creatinine are normal. She drinks about 1.5 L of fluid a day and eats a lot of processed food. Results of a 24-hour urine collection:

Urine (24 hours)ResultUsual goal
Volume1.6 L/dayabove 2.5 L/day
Calcium340 mg/daybelow 250 mg/day
Oxalate36 mg/daybelow 40 mg/day
Citrate620 mg/dayabove 450 mg/day
Uric acid560 mg/daybelow 750 mg/day
Sodium240 mEq/daybelow 100 mEq/day

Along with more fluid, which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: D
options.html: Potassium citrate and a high-oxalate diet

options.label: E
options.html: Sodium restriction, normal calcium intake and a thiazide diuretic

items.explanationHtml:
Her main metabolic risks are idiopathic hypercalciuria and low urine volume, worsened by a high sodium intake (sodium increases urine calcium). Treatment is more fluid, sodium restriction, a normal calcium intake (1,000–1,200 mg/day) and, because her stones recur, a thiazide, which increases distal calcium reabsorption and lowers urine calcium.

Takeaway: recurrent calcium stones with hypercalciuria: fluids, low sodium, normal calcium and a thiazide.

whyNot.A: Her urine uric acid is normal, so allopurinol is not indicated.
whyNot.B: Calcium restriction raises oxalate absorption and stone risk and harms bone.
whyNot.C: Loop diuretics increase urine calcium, and animal protein increases calcium excretion and lowers citrate.
whyNot.D: Her citrate is normal, and a high-oxalate diet would add to the risk.

items.objective: Prevent recurrent calcium oxalate stones from hypercalciuria with sodium restriction, normal calcium and a thiazide.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man is admitted with newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma with bulky abdominal disease. Leukocyte count is 28,000/mm³. Serum lactate dehydrogenase is 2,400 U/L (N = 45–200), uric acid 9.8 mg/dL, potassium 4.6 mEq/L, phosphorus 4.4 mg/dL and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. G6PD testing is normal. Intensive chemotherapy is to start tomorrow. Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to prevent kidney injury?

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous fluids and sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise urine

options.label: E
options.html: Restriction of oral fluids to prevent overload

items.explanationHtml:
Burkitt lymphoma with bulky disease, high LDH and a raised uric acid puts him at high risk of tumor lysis syndrome. Prevention is vigorous IV hydration plus rasburicase, a recombinant urate oxidase that converts uric acid to soluble allantoin and lowers it within hours. G6PD deficiency must be excluded first, because rasburicase produces hydrogen peroxide and can cause hemolysis and methemoglobinemia.

Takeaway: high-risk tumor lysis: IV fluids plus rasburicase (if G6PD is normal).

whyNot.B: Urine alkalinisation is no longer recommended: it favours calcium phosphate precipitation in the tubules.
whyNot.C: Allopurinol prevents new uric acid formation but does not remove existing uric acid; it suits intermediate risk.
whyNot.D: Dialysis is for established, refractory complications, not prevention.
whyNot.E: Fluid restriction would increase crystal precipitation; high urine flow is protective.

items.objective: Prevent tumor lysis syndrome in a high-risk patient with IV fluids and rasburicase.

items.stemHtml: He receives IV fluids and rasburicase, and chemotherapy begins. Forty-eight hours later he has had 150 mL of urine in 12 hours despite fluids and a trial of furosemide, and his lungs have bibasilar crackles. He has tingling around the mouth but no tetany or seizures. Serum potassium is 6.9 mEq/L, phosphorus 11.4 mg/dL, calcium 6.6 mg/dL, uric acid 3.1 mg/dL, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L and creatinine 4.3 mg/dL. ECG shows peaked T waves. Intravenous calcium gluconate, insulin with dextrose and albuterol are given. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Continuous intravenous calcium infusion to normalise calcium

items.explanationHtml:
He now has established tumor lysis syndrome with oliguric AKI, hyperkalemia with ECG changes, severe hyperphosphatemia, volume overload and acidosis. Temporising measures shift potassium only briefly, and with oliguria the kidneys cannot clear potassium or phosphate. Kidney replacement therapy (hemodialysis, or continuous therapy if unstable) is indicated.

Takeaway: tumor lysis with oliguria, refractory hyperkalemia, severe hyperphosphatemia or overload needs dialysis.

whyNot.A: Uric acid is already low; the current problems are potassium, phosphate, volume and oliguria.
whyNot.B: Large amounts of calcium with phosphate above 11 mg/dL risk calcium phosphate precipitation in tissues; calcium is given only for ECG protection or symptomatic hypocalcemia.
whyNot.D: A phosphate binder acts slowly and cannot address oliguria, overload or dangerous hyperkalemia.
whyNot.E: Tumor lysis is managed supportively; it is not a reason to abandon curative treatment of a highly curable lymphoma.

items.objective: Start dialysis for established tumor lysis syndrome with oliguric AKI and refractory electrolyte disorders.

items.stemHtml:
A 66-year-old man who smokes has blood pressure of 172/100 mm Hg despite three drugs. An epigastric bruit is heard. Serum potassium is 3.2 mEq/L and bicarbonate 30 mEq/L. Imaging shows 80% stenosis at the origin of the right renal artery and a normal left renal artery.

Plasma renin activityPlasma aldosteroneRenin in right renal vein vs left
AHighHighHigher
BHighLowLower
CLowHighEqual
DLowLowHigher
ENormalHighLower

Which of the following sets of findings is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
The poststenotic right kidney senses low perfusion pressure and releases renin, so its venous renin is higher than the left. Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone, producing secondary hyperaldosteronism (high renin and high aldosterone) with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. The normal left kidney, exposed to high pressure, suppresses its own renin.

Takeaway: unilateral renal artery stenosis gives high renin, high aldosterone, and lateralised renin from the stenotic side.

whyNot.B: Low aldosterone with high renin suggests adrenal insufficiency or aldosterone synthase deficiency, not renovascular disease.
whyNot.C: High aldosterone with low renin is primary aldosteronism; renin is not suppressed in renovascular hypertension.
whyNot.D: Low renin and low aldosterone fit mineralocorticoid excess from another hormone (such as Liddle syndrome or apparent mineralocorticoid excess), not stenosis.
whyNot.E: Renin is not normal here, and the stenotic kidney secretes more renin, not less.

items.objective: Predict renin and aldosterone findings in unilateral renal artery stenosis.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman has new hypertension (164/102 mm Hg). She has no family history of hypertension and takes no medications. A bruit is heard in the right upper abdomen. CT angiography shows alternating segments of narrowing and dilation in the middle and distal right renal artery. Which of the following best describes the most likely underlying lesion?

options.label: A
options.html: Atheromatous plaque with a necrotic lipid core

options.label: B
options.html: Granulomatous inflammation of the arterial wall with giant cells

options.label: D
options.html: Medial fibroplasia with thinned segments between fibrous ridges

options.label: E
options.html: Transmural necrotising inflammation with microaneurysms of medium arteries

items.explanationHtml:
A "string of beads" in the middle and distal renal artery of a young woman is fibromuscular dysplasia, most often the medial fibroplasia type: fibrous ridges alternate with thinned, aneurysmal segments of the media. It is noninflammatory and nonatherosclerotic.

Takeaway: young woman, mid-distal renal artery beading: fibromuscular dysplasia with medial fibroplasia.

whyNot.A: Atheroma affects the ostium and proximal artery in older patients with risk factors.
whyNot.B: Giant cell inflammation occurs in Takayasu arteritis, which narrows the aorta and the origins of its branches, with systemic symptoms and raised inflammatory markers.
whyNot.C: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a small-vessel change of long-standing hypertension and diabetes, not a main renal artery lesion.
whyNot.E: Polyarteritis nodosa causes microaneurysms and segmental necrosis of medium arteries, usually with systemic illness.

items.objective: Recognise fibromuscular dysplasia and its usual histologic type.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man with diabetes, peripheral artery disease and hypertension starts lisinopril. Two weeks later his serum creatinine has risen from 1.3 to 2.6 mg/dL. He is not volume depleted and takes no NSAIDs. Renal duplex ultrasonography later shows severe stenosis of both renal arteries. Which of the following best explains the rise in creatinine?

options.label: A
options.html: Angioedema of the renal arterial wall

options.label: B
options.html: Dilation of the afferent arteriole that raises glomerular pressure

options.label: C
options.html: Dilation of the efferent arteriole that lowers glomerular capillary pressure

options.label: D
options.html: Hyperkalemia that blocks proximal tubular creatinine secretion

options.label: E
options.html: Immune-mediated interstitial nephritis from the drug

items.explanationHtml:
When renal perfusion pressure is low, angiotensin II maintains GFR by constricting the efferent arteriole, which holds up glomerular capillary pressure. An ACE inhibitor removes that constriction; efferent dilation lowers glomerular pressure and GFR. With bilateral stenosis (or a solitary kidney) no kidney compensates, so creatinine rises sharply.

Takeaway: ACE inhibitors and ARBs lower GFR by dilating the efferent arteriole; a large creatinine rise suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis.

whyNot.A: Angioedema from ACE inhibitors involves the face, airway or bowel, not the renal artery.
whyNot.B: Afferent dilation would raise glomerular pressure and GFR; ACE inhibitors act mainly on the efferent side.
whyNot.D: Hyperkalemia does not block creatinine secretion; drugs such as trimethoprim and cimetidine do.
whyNot.E: Interstitial nephritis is rare with ACE inhibitors and would not be explained by the vascular finding.

items.objective: Explain the creatinine rise after ACE inhibition in bilateral renal artery stenosis.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman with a 30-year history of treated hypertension dies of a stroke. At autopsy both kidneys are symmetrically small with a finely granular cortical surface. Microscopy of the renal arterioles is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Concentric onion-skin layering of smooth muscle cells

options.label: D
options.html: Homogeneous pink glassy thickening of the walls with a narrowed lumen

items.explanationHtml:
Long-standing, moderate hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis: plasma proteins leak into the arteriolar wall and basement membrane material accumulates, giving homogeneous, glassy pink thickening that narrows the lumen. The resulting ischemia causes patchy glomerulosclerosis and tubular atrophy, so the kidneys shrink evenly with a finely granular surface (benign nephrosclerosis).

Takeaway: benign nephrosclerosis equals hyaline arteriolosclerosis and small granular kidneys.

whyNot.A: Onion-skin hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis is the lesion of malignant hypertension.
whyNot.B: Fibrinoid necrosis also marks malignant hypertension or vasculitis, not chronic stable hypertension.
whyNot.C: Granulomatous inflammation suggests a vasculitis such as giant cell arteritis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
whyNot.E: Needle-shaped clefts are cholesterol emboli, typically after arterial procedures.

items.objective: Identify hyaline arteriolosclerosis as the lesion of benign nephrosclerosis.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man stopped his antihypertensive drugs 6 months ago. He now has headache and blurred vision. Blood pressure is 238/142 mm Hg. Funduscopy shows papilledema and flame hemorrhages. Serum creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL, and a blood smear shows schistocytes. A kidney biopsy shows arterioles with concentric layers of smooth muscle cells and thickened basement membrane narrowing the lumen, and some arterioles with fibrinoid necrosis. Which of the following best describes the gross appearance of the kidney surface?

options.label: B
options.html: Pale wedge-shaped scar with its base at the capsule

options.label: C
options.html: Pinpoint hemorrhages scattered over the cortical surface

options.label: D
options.html: Symmetric coarse U-shaped scars over blunted calyces

options.label: E
options.html: Yellow nodules with a staghorn calculus in the pelvis

items.explanationHtml:
The biopsy shows hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis (onion-skinning) and fibrinoid necrosis: malignant nephrosclerosis from a hypertensive emergency. Ruptured arterioles and glomerular capillaries produce pinpoint petechial hemorrhages on the cortical surface, the "flea-bitten" kidney.

Takeaway: malignant hypertension: onion-skin arterioles, fibrinoid necrosis and a flea-bitten kidney surface.

whyNot.A: Large cysts replacing the parenchyma describe polycystic kidney disease.
whyNot.B: A wedge-shaped scar is a healed infarct from embolic or thrombotic arterial occlusion.
whyNot.D: Coarse scars over blunted calyces are typical of chronic pyelonephritis with reflux.
whyNot.E: Yellow nodules with a staghorn stone suggest xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis.

items.objective: Recognise the gross and microscopic kidney changes of malignant hypertension.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has had leg edema for 3 months. Urine protein is 9 g/day and serum albumin 1.8 g/dL. Kidney biopsy shows thickened glomerular capillary loops with subepithelial immune deposits and antibodies to the phospholipase A2 receptor. He now develops left flank pain, gross hematuria and a new left scrotal swelling that feels like a bag of worms. Urinary loss of which of the following most contributes to his new complication?
items.explanationHtml:
Membranous nephropathy carries the highest risk of renal vein thrombosis among causes of nephrotic syndrome. A key mechanism is urinary loss of the small anticoagulant protein antithrombin, while the liver increases synthesis of large procoagulants (fibrinogen, factors V and VIII) that are not filtered. Thrombosis of the left renal vein blocks drainage of the left gonadal vein, causing a new left varicocele.

Takeaway: nephrotic syndrome (especially membranous) promotes renal vein thrombosis partly by urinary antithrombin loss; a left renal vein clot can cause a left varicocele.

whyNot.B: Factor VIII is large and is increased, not lost, in nephrotic syndrome.
whyNot.C: Fibrinogen levels rise because hepatic synthesis increases; it is too large to be lost much in urine.
whyNot.D: PAI-1 is an antifibrinolytic; losing it would reduce, not increase, thrombosis.
whyNot.E: von Willebrand factor is a very large multimer that is not lost in urine and is usually raised.

items.objective: Explain the hypercoagulable state of nephrotic syndrome and renal vein thrombosis.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man had coronary angiography through the femoral artery 3 weeks ago. Since then his serum creatinine has risen from 1.2 to 2.8 mg/dL in steps. He has a lacy purple discolouration over both thighs and painful dusky toes with normal pedal pulses. Leukocyte count shows 9% eosinophils, and serum C3 is low. A kidney biopsy is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Crescents in most glomeruli with linear IgG staining

options.label: B
options.html: Elongated empty clefts in the lumens of arcuate and interlobular arteries

options.label: C
options.html: Fibrin thrombi in glomerular capillaries with no inflammation

options.label: D
options.html: Interstitial eosinophils and lymphocytes around normal arteries

options.label: E
options.html: Necrosis of proximal tubular cells with intact basement membranes only

items.explanationHtml:
Subacute, stepwise kidney failure weeks after an arterial procedure, with livedo reticularis, blue toes with preserved pulses, eosinophilia and hypocomplementemia, is atheroembolic (cholesterol crystal) kidney disease. Cholesterol crystals dissolve during tissue processing and leave biconvex, needle-shaped empty clefts in small arteries, surrounded by inflammation and later fibrosis.

Takeaway: after catheterisation, livedo plus eosinophilia plus slowly rising creatinine means cholesterol emboli with needle-shaped clefts.

whyNot.A: Linear IgG with crescents is anti-GBM disease, which does not follow catheterisation or cause livedo.
whyNot.C: Fibrin thrombi without crystals indicate a thrombotic microangiopathy.
whyNot.D: Allergic interstitial nephritis also causes eosinophilia, but not livedo or blue toes, and arteries are spared.
whyNot.E: Contrast-associated tubular injury appears within days and recovers; it does not cause livedo, eosinophilia or low complement.

items.objective: Recognise atheroembolic kidney disease and its biopsy finding.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old woman has had diffuse skin thickening of her hands, forearms, chest and face for 8 months, with antibodies to RNA polymerase III. She received prednisone 40 mg daily for 2 weeks for a myositis flare. She now has a severe headache. Blood pressure is 196/112 mm Hg (previously 118/76). Serum creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 2.4 mg/dL, and a blood smear shows schistocytes. Which of the following drugs acts on the main mechanism of her kidney injury?
items.explanationHtml:
This is scleroderma renal crisis: intimal proliferation narrows interlobular arteries, renal perfusion falls, and juxtaglomerular renin release surges, which drives severe hypertension and further vasoconstriction. Early diffuse disease, anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies and glucocorticoids raise the risk. An ACE inhibitor (captopril) blocks this renin-angiotensin loop and has transformed survival.

Takeaway: scleroderma renal crisis is renin driven; treat with an ACE inhibitor.

whyNot.B: Cyclophosphamide treats interstitial lung disease or vasculitis, not the renin-driven vasculopathy of renal crisis.
whyNot.C: Furosemide does not interrupt renin release and may worsen renal perfusion.
whyNot.D: Hydralazine lowers pressure but does not block the renin-angiotensin system that drives the crisis.
whyNot.E: High-dose glucocorticoids are a risk factor for renal crisis and may worsen it.

items.objective: Treat scleroderma renal crisis with an ACE inhibitor because it is renin driven.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old woman with long-standing atrial fibrillation who stopped her anticoagulant has sudden severe left flank pain and hematuria. She dies of a later stroke. At autopsy the left kidney contains a sharply demarcated, pale, triangular area whose base lies against the capsule. Which of the following best describes the change in this area?
items.explanationHtml:
Renal arteries are end arteries, so an embolus causes a wedge-shaped infarct with its base on the capsule. As in the heart and spleen, ischemic necrosis of a solid organ with a single blood supply is coagulative necrosis: cell outlines persist while nuclei disappear, and the infarct looks pale (white).

Takeaway: embolic renal infarcts are pale, wedge-shaped areas of coagulative necrosis.

whyNot.A: Caseous necrosis is the cheesy necrosis of tuberculosis and some fungal infections.
whyNot.C: Fat necrosis occurs in the pancreas and breast, from lipase action or trauma.
whyNot.D: Liquefactive necrosis occurs in the brain after ischemia and in abscesses.
whyNot.E: Red infarcts occur in organs with dual or collateral circulation (lung, intestine) or after venous occlusion, not in arterial kidney infarcts.

items.objective: Describe the pattern and type of necrosis in an embolic renal infarct.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with unilateral renal artery stenosis and hypertension is being evaluated for drug treatment. A drug is chosen that reduces renin release from juxtaglomerular cells by blocking their sympathetic stimulation. Which receptor does this drug block?
items.explanationHtml:
Sympathetic nerves stimulate renin release from juxtaglomerular cells through beta-1 adrenergic receptors (Gs, rising cAMP). Beta-blockers therefore lower plasma renin, which contributes to their antihypertensive effect. The other two triggers of renin release are low afferent arteriolar pressure and low sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa.

Takeaway: beta-1 stimulation of juxtaglomerular cells releases renin; beta-blockers suppress it.

whyNot.A: Alpha-1 receptors constrict vascular smooth muscle; blocking them lowers resistance but does not suppress renin (it can raise it reflexly).
whyNot.B: Central alpha-2 agonists (not blockers) reduce sympathetic outflow; alpha-2 blockade would raise sympathetic tone.
whyNot.C: AT1 blockers act downstream of renin and cause renin to rise by removing negative feedback.
whyNot.E: Juxtaglomerular renin release is not controlled by muscarinic receptors.

items.objective: Identify the receptor that mediates sympathetic renin release.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man has hypertension controlled on amlodipine, lisinopril and chlorthalidone. He has coronary artery disease and quit smoking 5 years ago. He has had no episodes of pulmonary edema. Serum creatinine has been stable at 1.4 mg/dL for 2 years. CT angiography done for a suspected abdominal aortic aneurysm shows 75% stenosis at the origin of the left renal artery; kidney sizes are 11.2 cm on the right and 10.6 cm on the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue his drugs and add a high-intensity statin and aspirin

options.label: B
options.html: Left renal artery angioplasty with stent placement

options.label: C
options.html: Laparoscopic left nephrectomy to remove the renin source

options.label: D
options.html: Stop lisinopril and replace it with hydralazine

options.label: E
options.html: Surgical aortorenal bypass of the left renal artery

items.explanationHtml:
He has atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis with controlled blood pressure, stable kidney function and no flash pulmonary edema. Trials comparing stenting plus medical therapy with medical therapy alone showed no reduction in cardiovascular or renal events, so the right approach is optimal medical therapy: continue the ACE inhibitor (unilateral disease, stable creatinine), add a high-intensity statin and an antiplatelet agent, and keep risk factors controlled.

Takeaway: most atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis is treated medically; revascularise only for specific triggers.

whyNot.B: Stenting adds procedural risk without benefit in a patient with controlled pressure and stable function.
whyNot.C: Nephrectomy is not indicated for a functioning kidney with a stenosis.
whyNot.D: An ACE inhibitor is well tolerated here and protective; there is no reason to stop it.
whyNot.E: Surgical bypass is reserved for complex anatomy needing revascularisation, which he does not need.

items.objective: Manage incidental atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis with optimal medical therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman has had hypertension (158/98 mm Hg) for 4 months despite amlodipine. She takes no other medications or supplements and has no headaches with palpitations. Serum potassium is 3.6 mEq/L and creatinine 0.7 mg/dL. CT angiography shows a beaded appearance of the mid right renal artery with about 70% narrowing and no aneurysm; cervical and intracranial arteries are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Add an ACE inhibitor and recheck in 1 year

items.explanationHtml:
Hypertension from renal fibromuscular dysplasia in a young woman is the classic indication for percutaneous transluminal angioplasty, usually without a stent. It often cures or markedly improves the hypertension, especially when the hypertension is of short duration.

Takeaway: renovascular hypertension from fibromuscular dysplasia is treated with balloon angioplasty without stenting.

whyNot.A: Drug therapy alone leaves a correctable cause untreated in a young patient who could be cured.
whyNot.C: Stents are reserved for complications such as dissection during angioplasty; they are not routine in fibromuscular dysplasia.
whyNot.D: Nephrectomy is not appropriate for a functioning kidney with a treatable lesion.
whyNot.E: Fibromuscular dysplasia is not inflammatory; glucocorticoids are used for arteritis.

items.objective: Treat hypertension from renal fibromuscular dysplasia with angioplasty without a stent.

items.stemHtml: A 51-year-old woman with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis diagnosed 1 year ago has headache and fatigue for 2 days. Blood pressure is 188/110 mm Hg (usually 120/78). Serum creatinine is 2.2 mg/dL (0.9 mg/dL a month ago). Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL with schistocytes on the smear, and platelets are 96,000/mm³. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein and a few red cells. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Captopril, titrated up every few hours to control blood pressure

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous labetalol, aiming at normal blood pressure within 1 hour

items.explanationHtml:
New severe hypertension, rising creatinine and microangiopathic hemolysis early in diffuse systemic sclerosis is scleroderma renal crisis. Start a short-acting ACE inhibitor (captopril) and titrate quickly, aiming for gradual blood pressure reduction, and continue it even if creatinine rises or dialysis is needed. Other agents such as calcium channel blockers are added only if pressure stays high on the maximum ACE inhibitor dose.

Takeaway: scleroderma renal crisis is treated with a rapidly titrated ACE inhibitor, continued even on dialysis.

whyNot.B: Beta-blockers do not address the renin-angiotensin drive, and dropping pressure to normal within an hour risks ischemia.
whyNot.C: Glucocorticoids can precipitate or worsen scleroderma renal crisis.
whyNot.D: Plasma exchange is the treatment for TTP; this microangiopathy is caused by the scleroderma vasculopathy.
whyNot.E: Rituximab has no role in the acute crisis.

items.objective: Treat scleroderma renal crisis with a titrated ACE inhibitor.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old man had an aortic aneurysm repaired by an endovascular approach 4 weeks ago. Since then serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.5 mg/dL. He has a mottled, lacy rash on his legs and two painful purple toes with palpable pedal pulses. Eosinophils are 8% of leukocytes. Urinalysis shows a few white cells, no red cell casts and 1+ protein. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Renal artery angiography with stent placement

options.label: D
options.html: Supportive care with blood pressure control and a statin

items.explanationHtml:
This is atheroembolic kidney disease, caused by cholesterol crystals dislodged from the aorta during the procedure. No therapy dissolves the crystals. Management is supportive: blood pressure control, a statin and aspirin, avoidance of further arterial procedures and anticoagulation when possible, and dialysis if needed.

Takeaway: atheroembolic kidney disease is treated supportively; avoid anticoagulation and further procedures when possible.

whyNot.A: Glucocorticoids have no proven benefit for cholesterol embolisation.
whyNot.B: Anticoagulation may promote further plaque instability and embolisation.
whyNot.C: More catheter manipulation risks further embolisation; the problem is in small arteries, not a main renal artery lesion.
whyNot.E: Thrombolysis does not dissolve cholesterol crystals and adds bleeding risk.

items.objective: Manage atheroembolic kidney disease supportively.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation stopped apixaban 2 weeks ago before a dental procedure and did not restart it. She has had sudden, constant right flank pain for 8 hours with nausea. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse 104/min and irregular, and blood pressure 156/92 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows 15 red cells per high-power field. Serum LDH is 1,450 U/L (N = 45–200 U/L), and AST and ALT are normal. Noncontrast CT shows no stone or hydronephrosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the abdomen with intravenous contrast (CT angiography)

items.explanationHtml:
Acute flank pain, hematuria and a strikingly high LDH with normal aminotransferases in a patient with atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation suggest renal infarction. Noncontrast CT excludes a stone but cannot show perfusion; contrast-enhanced CT (CT angiography) shows a wedge-shaped perfusion defect and the occluded branch.

Takeaway: suspect renal infarction when flank pain with hematuria and high LDH has no stone; confirm with contrast CT.

whyNot.B: Cystoscopy evaluates bladder sources of hematuria, not acute flank pain from an embolus.
whyNot.C: Biopsy is not needed, and is hazardous in an infarcted kidney.
whyNot.D: Repeating a noncontrast study will still not show the perfusion defect and delays treatment.
whyNot.E: She has no fever or pyuria to suggest pyelonephritis, and culture would not explain the LDH.

items.objective: Confirm suspected renal infarction with contrast-enhanced CT.

items.stemHtml: CT angiography shows a wedge-shaped area of absent enhancement in the lower pole of the right kidney and an abrupt cutoff of a segmental renal artery branch. Serum creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. Echocardiography shows no left ventricular thrombus. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Anticoagulation with heparin, then long-term oral anticoagulation

options.label: E
options.html: Surgical embolectomy of the segmental branch

items.explanationHtml:
An embolic segmental renal infarction with preserved function is treated with anticoagulation, starting with heparin and continuing long-term oral anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation to prevent further renal and systemic emboli. Catheter-directed therapy is reserved for selected early, main-artery occlusions.

Takeaway: embolic renal infarction is treated with anticoagulation and secondary prevention of emboli.

whyNot.B: Aspirin alone is inadequate stroke and embolism prevention in atrial fibrillation.
whyNot.C: Nephrectomy is not needed for a segmental infarct in a functioning kidney.
whyNot.D: Without anticoagulation she remains at high risk of stroke and further emboli.
whyNot.E: Open embolectomy of a small segmental branch is not done; the infarcted tissue cannot be salvaged this way.

items.objective: Treat embolic renal infarction with anticoagulation.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his car was struck from the side. He has a pelvic ring fracture with symphysis diastasis. He cannot void. There is blood at the urethral meatus and a perineal hematoma, and on rectal examination the prostate cannot be felt in its usual position. Which part of the urinary tract is most likely injured?
items.explanationHtml:
Shearing forces in a pelvic fracture tear the posterior urethra, usually at the membranous segment where it passes through the urogenital diaphragm just below the prostate. The prostate and bladder are pushed upward by the hematoma, so the prostate feels high-riding or cannot be felt.

Takeaway: pelvic fracture with blood at the meatus and a high-riding prostate means posterior (membranous) urethral injury.

whyNot.A: A blow to a full bladder tears the dome (intraperitoneal rupture); it does not cause blood at the meatus with a displaced prostate.
whyNot.B: The bulbar urethra is injured by straddle injuries, crushing it against the pubic bone, not by pelvic fracture shearing.
whyNot.D: Penile urethral injury follows direct penile trauma such as penile fracture.
whyNot.E: The ureterovesical junction lies deep in the pelvis and is rarely injured by blunt trauma; it would not cause blood at the meatus.

items.objective: Localise urethral injury after pelvic fracture to the membranous urethra.

items.stemHtml: An 11-year-old boy slipped while climbing a fence and landed astride the top rail. Several hours later he has perineal pain and swelling and a few drops of blood at the urethral meatus. Over the next day, swelling and bruising spread across the perineum, scrotum and penis and up onto the lower anterior abdominal wall. The swelling stops at a sharp line at the top of each thigh. Which of the following best explains this boundary?

options.label: A
options.html: Attachment of the membranous layer of superficial fascia to the fascia lata

options.label: B
options.html: Attachment of the perineal membrane to the ischiopubic rami

options.label: C
options.html: Continuity of Buck fascia with the tunica albuginea

options.label: D
options.html: Fusion of the external spermatic fascia with the cremaster

options.label: E
options.html: The tendinous arch of the levator ani muscle

items.explanationHtml:
A straddle injury tears the bulbar urethra. When Buck fascia is breached, blood and urine collect in the superficial perineal space beneath Colles fascia, which is continuous with the scrotal dartos and with Scarpa fascia on the abdominal wall. Laterally, the membranous layer fuses with the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament, which keeps the fluid out of the thighs.

Takeaway: extravasation from a bulbar urethral tear spreads to the scrotum, penis and abdominal wall but not the thighs, because Colles and Scarpa fascia attach to the fascia lata.

whyNot.B: The perineal membrane bounds the space posteriorly and deeply, which keeps fluid from passing backward or into the deep pouch; it does not explain the lateral limit at the thighs.
whyNot.C: If Buck fascia were intact, the hematoma would stay confined to the penile shaft; its continuity with the tunica albuginea does not limit spread to the thighs.
whyNot.D: Spermatic cord fascial layers do not determine the lateral boundary of superficial perineal extravasation.
whyNot.E: The levator ani arch bounds the pelvic floor, above the urogenital region, and is not involved in superficial extravasation.

items.objective: Explain the fascial limits of urine extravasation after bulbar urethral injury.

items.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 20 hours after a bicycle crash in which the handlebar struck his lower abdomen. He had been drinking beer for several hours beforehand. He has diffuse abdominal pain and distension and has passed only a small amount of blood-tinged urine. Blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Serum urea nitrogen is 52 mg/dL and creatinine 3.1 mg/dL; a year ago creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL. CT cystography shows contrast outlining loops of small bowel. Which of the following best explains the laboratory findings?

options.label: B
options.html: Bilateral ureteral obstruction by pelvic hematoma

options.label: E
options.html: Reabsorption of urine solutes across the peritoneum

items.explanationHtml:
A blow to a full bladder ruptures the dome into the peritoneal cavity. Urea and creatinine in the leaked urine diffuse back into the blood across the large peritoneal surface, so serum levels climb even when the kidneys work normally. Repair of the bladder corrects the values.

Takeaway: intraperitoneal bladder rupture can raise serum urea nitrogen and creatinine by peritoneal reabsorption of urine.

whyNot.A: Rhabdomyolysis follows crush injury or prolonged immobilisation; nothing suggests muscle injury here, and the cystogram explains the picture.
whyNot.B: Pelvic hematoma severe enough to obstruct both ureters would accompany a major pelvic fracture, and the CT shows a bladder leak instead.
whyNot.C: Contrast nephropathy, if it occurs, appears 24–72 hours after contrast, not on the arrival tests that preceded imaging.
whyNot.D: His blood pressure is normal, and hemorrhage would not explain the urine leak shown on cystography.

items.objective: Explain the pseudo-renal failure of intraperitoneal bladder rupture.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man has a complete spinal cord injury at the T8 level from a fall 6 months ago. He now has frequent leakage of small volumes of urine between catheterisations and two febrile UTIs. Renal ultrasonography shows bilateral hydronephrosis and a thick-walled, trabeculated bladder. Which of the following findings on urodynamic testing is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Absent detrusor contractions with a large, compliant bladder

options.label: B
options.html: Detrusor contractions with simultaneous contraction of the external sphincter

options.label: C
options.html: Normal detrusor activity with an open bladder neck at rest

options.label: D
options.html: Normal storage pressure with a weak external sphincter

options.label: E
options.html: Uninhibited detrusor contractions with coordinated sphincter relaxation

items.explanationHtml:
A spinal cord lesion between the pontine micturition centre and the sacral cord cuts the pathway that coordinates voiding. After spinal shock, reflex detrusor contractions return, but the external sphincter contracts at the same time: detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia. The resulting high pressures thicken the bladder wall and cause reflux, hydronephrosis and infection.

Takeaway: suprasacral spinal cord injury gives detrusor overactivity with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, which threatens the upper tracts.

whyNot.A: An areflexic, large bladder results from sacral cord, cauda equina or peripheral nerve lesions, or from the early spinal shock phase.
whyNot.C: An open bladder neck at rest suggests sympathetic denervation or prior surgery and would not explain trabeculation and hydronephrosis.
whyNot.D: Low storage pressure with sphincter weakness causes stress-type leakage without upper-tract damage.
whyNot.E: Overactivity with coordinated relaxation is the pattern of lesions above the pons, such as stroke, where the pontine centre still coordinates voiding.

items.objective: Predict detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia after suprasacral spinal cord injury.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman with a 25-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus has constant dribbling of urine, a weak stream and a feeling of incomplete emptying. She has numbness of both feet to the ankles and orthostatic hypotension. Post-void residual volume is 520 mL (normal below 100 mL). Loss of function of which of the following is the most likely cause of her urinary symptoms?

options.label: A
options.html: Hypogastric sympathetic fibres to the bladder neck

options.label: B
options.html: Pelvic splanchnic fibres to the detrusor

options.label: D
options.html: Pudendal motor fibres to the external sphincter

options.label: E
options.html: Upper motor neurons in the lateral corticospinal tract

items.explanationHtml:
Long-standing diabetes damages autonomic and sensory fibres. Loss of bladder sensation and of the parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic (S2–S4) input that contracts the detrusor leaves an underactive, overdistended bladder that empties poorly; urine leaks when pressure exceeds outlet resistance (overflow incontinence).

Takeaway: diabetic autonomic neuropathy causes an underactive detrusor with retention and overflow incontinence.

whyNot.A: Loss of sympathetic tone would open the bladder neck and impair storage, not cause retention with a large residual.
whyNot.C: Damage to the pontine centre would cause uncoordinated voiding, and diabetes does not selectively injure it.
whyNot.D: Pudendal motor loss weakens the external sphincter and causes stress-type leakage, not a large post-void residual.
whyNot.E: Upper motor neuron lesions give an overactive (spastic) bladder, not an atonic one.

items.objective: Explain overflow incontinence from diabetic autonomic neuropathy.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman with overactive bladder is started on a drug that relaxes the detrusor during bladder filling by stimulating a Gs-coupled receptor and raising intracellular cAMP. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
items.explanationHtml:
Mirabegron (and vibegron) are beta-3 adrenergic agonists. Beta-3 receptors on the detrusor couple to Gs, raise cAMP and relax the smooth muscle during storage, increasing bladder capacity. They avoid anticholinergic adverse effects but can raise blood pressure.

Takeaway: beta-3 agonists (mirabegron, vibegron) relax the detrusor through Gs and cAMP and treat overactive bladder without anticholinergic effects.

whyNot.A: Bethanechol is a muscarinic agonist that contracts the detrusor; it is used for urinary retention, not overactive bladder.
whyNot.C: Oxybutynin relaxes the detrusor by blocking M3 (G<sub>q</sub>) receptors, not by stimulating a G<sub>s</sub> receptor.
whyNot.D: Tamsulosin blocks alpha-1A receptors in the prostate and bladder neck to ease outflow obstruction.
whyNot.E: Tolterodine is a muscarinic antagonist, not a G<sub>s</sub>-coupled receptor agonist.

items.objective: Identify the mechanism of beta-3 agonists for overactive bladder.

items.stemHtml: A 2-day-old boy born at 36 weeks has a palpable distended bladder and a weak, dribbling urinary stream. Prenatal ultrasonography at 30 weeks showed oligohydramnios, bilateral hydronephrosis and a dilated bladder with a dilated proximal urethra. He needed brief respiratory support at birth. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.label: C
options.html: Membranous folds obstructing the posterior urethra

options.label: D
options.html: Neurogenic bladder from a sacral neural tube defect

items.explanationHtml:
Posterior urethral valves are obstructing folds in the prostatic urethra of boys. Obstruction below the bladder dilates the posterior urethra (the "keyhole" sign), thickens the bladder and causes bilateral hydronephrosis. Reduced fetal urine output causes oligohydramnios, which can impair lung development. Voiding cystourethrography confirms the diagnosis, and treatment is catheter drainage then endoscopic valve ablation.

Takeaway: a boy with a distended bladder, dilated posterior urethra, bilateral hydronephrosis and oligohydramnios has posterior urethral valves.

whyNot.A: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction dilates the renal pelvis but leaves the bladder and urethra normal.
whyNot.B: Reflux alone does not distend the bladder or dilate the posterior urethra, and it does not cause a weak stream.
whyNot.D: A sacral neural tube defect would be visible on examination of the back and would usually cause other lower limb or anal findings.
whyNot.E: Meatal stenosis affects the external opening and is a problem of circumcised older boys; it does not dilate the posterior urethra.

items.objective: Recognise posterior urethral valves from prenatal and neonatal findings.

items.stemHtml: A 78-year-old man with prostatic enlargement has a urinary catheter placed for painless retention of 2,100 mL. Serum creatinine falls from 4.8 to 2.0 mg/dL over 2 days, but his urine output is 400–500 mL/h. Urine osmolality is 280 mOsm/kg. Which of the following best explains the urine output?

options.label: A
options.html: Excess antidiuretic hormone release from pain

options.label: C
options.html: Overproduction of aldosterone after obstruction is relieved

options.label: D
options.html: Retained urea excretion plus impaired tubular concentrating ability

options.label: E
options.html: Spontaneous bladder hyperactivity after catheter placement

items.explanationHtml:
Post-obstructive diuresis follows relief of bilateral obstruction (or obstruction of a solitary kidney). Part is appropriate: the kidney excretes the urea, salt and water retained during obstruction. Part is maladaptive: obstruction washes out medullary tonicity and lowers aquaporin-2 and sodium transporter expression, so the tubules cannot concentrate urine for days.

Takeaway: post-obstructive diuresis reflects solute (urea) excretion plus a temporary concentrating defect; monitor volume and electrolytes.

whyNot.A: Antidiuretic hormone would concentrate urine and reduce output.
whyNot.B: Nothing suggests hyperglycemia, and glucose-driven diuresis needs very high serum glucose.
whyNot.C: Aldosterone would reduce sodium and water excretion, not increase it.
whyNot.E: Detrusor activity does not determine urine production by the kidneys; a catheter drains whatever the kidneys make.

items.objective: Explain the mechanisms of post-obstructive diuresis.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman, para 3, has leaked small amounts of urine when she coughs, sneezes or lifts her children since her last vaginal delivery, which involved a prolonged second stage and forceps. She has no urgency. Injury to which of the following nerves most directly contributes to weakness of the external urethral sphincter in this setting?
items.explanationHtml:
The external urethral sphincter and the levator ani are skeletal muscles supplied by somatic fibres from S2–S4. The pudendal nerve supplies the external sphincter, and stretch injury to it during a prolonged or instrumented vaginal delivery, together with direct pelvic floor damage, contributes to stress incontinence.

Takeaway: the pudendal nerve (S2–S4) supplies the external urethral sphincter; its injury in childbirth contributes to stress incontinence.

whyNot.A: The genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster and skin of the anterior genitalia and thigh.
whyNot.B: The iliohypogastric nerve supplies skin and muscles of the lower anterior abdominal wall.
whyNot.C: The obturator nerve supplies the medial thigh adductors.
whyNot.D: Pelvic splanchnic nerves are parasympathetic fibres that contract the detrusor; they do not supply the skeletal muscle sphincter.

items.objective: Link pudendal nerve injury in childbirth to stress urinary incontinence.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a motorcycle crash. After resuscitation with 1 L of crystalloid, his pulse is 104/min and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. Pelvic radiography shows bilateral superior and inferior pubic rami fractures. There is blood at the urethral meatus and a scrotal hematoma. He has not voided. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast

options.label: D
options.html: Suprapubic aspiration of urine for culture

items.explanationHtml:
Blood at the meatus after a pelvic fracture means a urethral injury until proven otherwise. A retrograde urethrogram must come before any urethral catheter, because passing a catheter blindly can convert a partial tear into a complete one and introduce infection into the hematoma.

Takeaway: suspected urethral injury: retrograde urethrogram before a Foley catheter.

whyNot.A: CT may be needed for other injuries, but it does not evaluate the urethra, and he will still need a safe route to drain his bladder.
whyNot.B: A urethral catheter before the urethra is imaged risks worsening the injury.
whyNot.D: Aspiration for culture has no role in acute trauma.
whyNot.E: Voiding cystourethrography needs a catheter in the bladder first and is used for reflux and valves in children.

items.objective: Order a retrograde urethrogram before catheterisation when urethral injury is suspected.

items.stemHtml: The retrograde urethrogram shows extravasation of contrast at the membranous urethra with no contrast entering the bladder. His vital signs remain stable, and CT of the abdomen shows no other injury. His bladder is palpable above the pubic symphysis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in bladder management?

options.label: C
options.html: Repeated attempts at urethral catheterisation with a coudé catheter

options.label: E
options.html: Intravenous furosemide to maintain urine output

items.explanationHtml:
A complete posterior urethral disruption means urine cannot pass and a urethral catheter cannot be placed safely. A suprapubic cystostomy drains the bladder. Definitive repair is usually delayed for about 3 months (delayed urethroplasty) once the hematoma has resolved, or early endoscopic realignment is done in selected patients by a urologist.

Takeaway: complete urethral disruption: drain with a suprapubic catheter and repair the urethra later.

whyNot.A: Immediate open repair through a fresh pelvic hematoma has high rates of bleeding, impotence and incontinence.
whyNot.C: Blind repeated catheterisation risks false passages and enlarging the tear.
whyNot.D: He cannot void through a disrupted urethra; waiting allows painful overdistension.
whyNot.E: Diuretics would worsen bladder distension without a route for drainage.

items.objective: Manage complete posterior urethral disruption with suprapubic cystostomy.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman is struck by a car while crossing the street. She is alert. Pulse is 96/min and blood pressure 126/80 mm Hg. She has lower abdominal tenderness and gross hematuria. CT shows no pelvic fracture or solid-organ injury. CT cystography with retrograde filling of the bladder through a catheter shows contrast tracking between loops of small bowel and into both paracolic gutters. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Bladder catheter drainage alone for 14 days

items.explanationHtml:
Contrast around bowel loops and in the paracolic gutters shows an intraperitoneal bladder rupture, usually a tear of the dome. Urine continues to leak into the peritoneum, causing peritonitis and metabolic derangement, so it needs operative repair (open or laparoscopic) with bladder drainage afterwards.

Takeaway: intraperitoneal bladder rupture needs surgical repair; most extraperitoneal ruptures heal with catheter drainage.

whyNot.A: Embolisation controls arterial bleeding; there is no active hemorrhage described.
whyNot.B: Catheter drainage alone is the treatment for uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture, not intraperitoneal rupture.
whyNot.C: Fulguration treats bleeding mucosal lesions, not full-thickness tears.
whyNot.D: Peritoneal lavage is a dated diagnostic test; the diagnosis is already made.

items.objective: Treat intraperitoneal bladder rupture surgically.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being tackled during a football game. He has left flank pain and gross hematuria. Pulse is 88/min and blood pressure 130/78 mm Hg, unchanged over 2 hours. Hemoglobin is 13.8 g/dL. Contrast CT with delayed images shows a 2-cm-deep laceration of the left renal cortex extending into the collecting system with a small amount of urinary contrast leak, a perirenal hematoma confined by Gerota fascia, and no active arterial contrast extravasation. The right kidney is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Admission for bed rest, serial hemoglobin measurement and observation

options.label: D
options.html: Immediate placement of a left percutaneous nephrostomy

options.label: E
options.html: Selective angioembolisation of the left renal artery branch

items.explanationHtml:
This is a high-grade (collecting-system) renal laceration in a hemodynamically stable patient without active bleeding. Nonoperative management (admission, bed rest, serial hemoglobin, repeat imaging if symptoms change) preserves the kidney in most such cases; many urine leaks seal, and a ureteral stent is placed only if a leak persists or grows.

Takeaway: stable renal trauma, even high grade, is managed nonoperatively; embolise active bleeding and operate for instability.

whyNot.B: Nephrectomy is for an unreconstructable kidney in an unstable patient.
whyNot.C: Exploration is for hemodynamic instability or an expanding hematoma, and it raises the chance of losing the kidney.
whyNot.D: Most urine leaks seal; drainage is reserved for persistent or enlarging collections.
whyNot.E: Angioembolisation is for active contrast extravasation or a pseudoaneurysm, which is absent here.

items.objective: Manage a stable high-grade renal laceration nonoperatively.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment has 6 months of sudden, strong urges to void with leakage before she reaches the toilet, about four times daily, and nocturia twice nightly. She does not leak with coughing. Urinalysis is normal and post-void residual volume is 40 mL. She completed 8 weeks of bladder training and reduced her evening fluids and caffeine with partial improvement, and she wants further treatment. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
She has urge incontinence (overactive bladder) with only partial response to behavioural therapy. Drug therapy is reasonable, and in an older adult with cognitive impairment a beta-3 agonist (vibegron or mirabegron) is preferred over antimuscarinics, which add to anticholinergic burden and can worsen cognition, constipation and falls.

Takeaway: for overactive bladder in an older adult with cognitive concerns, choose a beta-3 agonist over an antimuscarinic.

whyNot.A: Intermittent catheterisation treats retention with a large residual; her residual is normal.
whyNot.B: Desmopressin reduces urine production, does not treat detrusor overactivity, and is generally avoided at this age because of the risk of hyponatremia.
whyNot.C: A sling treats stress incontinence, which she does not have.
whyNot.D: Oxybutynin is strongly anticholinergic and is best avoided in an older adult with cognitive impairment.

items.objective: Choose a beta-3 agonist for overactive bladder in an older adult with cognitive impairment.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman, para 2, has leaked urine with coughing, running and lifting for a year. She has no urgency, nocturia or dysuria. BMI is 31 kg/m². Pelvic examination shows leakage of urine with a cough while supine, with mild urethral hypermobility and no prolapse beyond the hymen. Urinalysis is normal and post-void residual volume is 30 mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
This is stress urinary incontinence. First-line treatment is supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months, with weight loss because obesity raises intra-abdominal pressure. A pessary or urethral insert is another conservative option; a midurethral sling is offered if conservative treatment does not satisfy her.

Takeaway: first-line treatment for stress incontinence is pelvic floor muscle training (plus weight loss); surgery comes after conservative treatment.

whyNot.A: OnabotulinumtoxinA treats refractory overactive bladder, not stress incontinence.
whyNot.B: A sling is effective but is offered after conservative treatment, or for a patient who declines it.
whyNot.D: Antimuscarinics treat urge incontinence and do not strengthen the outlet.
whyNot.E: Alpha blockers relax the bladder neck and could worsen stress leakage.

items.objective: Start pelvic floor muscle training for stress urinary incontinence.

items.stemHtml:
A 64-year-old man with spina bifida treated in infancy has a long-standing neurogenic bladder. He voids by straining and has had two febrile UTIs this year. Results:

TestResult
Post-void residual volume (bladder scan)480 mL (normal below 100 mL)
UrodynamicsLarge-capacity bladder, no detrusor contraction during attempted voiding
Serum creatinine1.3 mg/dL (1 year ago 1.0 mg/dL)
Renal ultrasonographyMild bilateral hydronephrosis; no stones

He has good hand function and is willing to learn self-care. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term bladder management?
items.explanationHtml:
An areflexic detrusor with a large residual, recurrent infection, hydronephrosis and rising creatinine needs regular, complete emptying. Clean intermittent self-catheterisation every 4–6 hours is the standard: it protects the kidneys and causes fewer infections and urethral complications than an indwelling catheter.

Takeaway: for an underactive neurogenic bladder with a large residual, use clean intermittent catheterisation.

whyNot.A: Bethanechol is ineffective for long-term emptying of an areflexic bladder and causes cholinergic adverse effects.
whyNot.C: Indwelling urethral catheters cause more infections, stones, strictures and urethral erosion and are a last resort.
whyNot.D: A beta-3 agonist relaxes the detrusor further and would worsen retention.
whyNot.E: Timed voiding does not help when the detrusor cannot contract.

items.objective: Use clean intermittent catheterisation for an areflexic neurogenic bladder.

items.stemHtml: A 15-month-old girl had her first febrile UTI 2 weeks ago, with a temperature of 39.4°C (102.9°F) and pyuria; urine obtained by catheter grew more than 100,000 CFU/mL of E. coli. She recovered with oral cephalexin. Renal and bladder ultrasonography today shows moderate dilation of the left renal pelvis and a dilated left distal ureter. The right kidney is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Long-term trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis without further imaging

items.explanationHtml:
After a first febrile UTI in a young child, renal and bladder ultrasonography comes first. Because it shows hydronephrosis with a dilated ureter, which suggests high-grade vesicoureteral reflux or obstruction, the next step is voiding cystourethrography to look for and grade reflux and to assess the urethra.

Takeaway: abnormal ultrasound after a first febrile UTI in a toddler calls for voiding cystourethrography.

whyNot.A: CT exposes a child to radiation and does not show reflux.
whyNot.B: Whether prophylaxis is indicated depends on the reflux grade, which is not yet known.
whyNot.C: Normal ultrasound would allow watchful waiting, but hers is abnormal.
whyNot.D: A DMSA scan shows renal scarring but does not diagnose or grade reflux.

items.objective: Order voiding cystourethrography when ultrasound is abnormal after a first febrile UTI in a young child.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old girl with short stature, a webbed neck and primary amenorrhea has a karyotype of 45,X. Renal ultrasonography shows the lower poles of both kidneys joined by a band of tissue anterior to the aorta, lying lower than usual. Which of the following structures most likely prevented normal ascent of these kidneys?
items.explanationHtml:
In a horseshoe kidney, the fused lower poles form an isthmus that catches under the inferior mesenteric artery as the kidneys ascend from the pelvis, so the kidneys sit low in the abdomen. It is common in Turner syndrome.

Takeaway: horseshoe kidneys are trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery; think Turner syndrome.

whyNot.A: The celiac trunk arises far above the level reached by the kidneys and does not block their ascent.
whyNot.C: The median sacral artery arises at the aortic bifurcation, below the level of the isthmus.
whyNot.D: The superior mesenteric artery lies above the inferior mesenteric artery; horseshoe kidneys stop below it.
whyNot.E: The gonadal arteries descend lateral to the kidneys and do not form a barrier across the midline.

items.objective: Explain the low position of a horseshoe kidney and its association with Turner syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A male newborn delivered at 34 weeks dies 2 hours after birth despite intubation and ventilation. Prenatal ultrasonography at 20 weeks showed anhydramnios, and neither kidney nor the bladder could be seen. At birth he had widely spaced eyes, a flattened nose, low-set ears and bilateral clubfoot. Which of the following is the most likely direct cause of death?
items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral renal agenesis means no fetal urine and therefore almost no amniotic fluid from the second trimester. The resulting Potter sequence includes facial compression, limb deformities and, most important, pulmonary hypoplasia, because the lungs need amniotic fluid to develop. Respiratory failure, not renal failure, causes death within hours.

Takeaway: oligohydramnios from absent fetal urine causes Potter sequence; death is from pulmonary hypoplasia.

whyNot.A: Nothing suggests a diaphragmatic defect; the findings are those of oligohydramnios.
whyNot.B: Potassium rises over days without kidneys; the placenta cleared solutes before birth, so it cannot explain death at 2 hours.
whyNot.C: Sepsis does not explain the prenatal findings or death within 2 hours of birth.
whyNot.E: Uremia takes days to develop after birth because the placenta did the kidney's work in utero.

items.objective: Identify pulmonary hypoplasia as the lethal consequence of bilateral renal agenesis.

items.stemHtml: In a study of human kidney development, cells from the ureteric bud are labelled at week 5 and traced into the mature kidney. Which of the following structures will contain labelled cells?

options.label: E
options.html: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

items.explanationHtml:
The ureteric bud branches to form the ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts. The nephron itself, from Bowman capsule through the distal convoluted tubule, comes from the metanephric mesenchyme; glomerular capillaries come from ingrowing endothelial precursors.

Takeaway: ureteric bud gives the collecting system (collecting ducts to ureter); metanephric mesenchyme gives the nephron up to the distal tubule.

whyNot.A: Bowman capsule forms from metanephric mesenchyme.
whyNot.C: The distal convoluted tubule is the last nephron segment derived from metanephric mesenchyme.
whyNot.D: Glomerular endothelium comes from angioblasts that migrate into the developing glomerulus, not from the bud.
whyNot.E: The loop of Henle, including the thick ascending limb, is derived from metanephric mesenchyme.

items.objective: Distinguish ureteric bud from metanephric mesenchyme derivatives.

items.stemHtml: In mouse embryos lacking a receptor tyrosine kinase expressed on the epithelium of the ureteric bud, the bud fails to grow into the metanephric mesenchyme and both kidneys are absent. Which of the following signalling molecules, secreted by the metanephric mesenchyme, normally activates this receptor?

options.label: B
options.html: Fibroblast growth factor 8 from the apical ectodermal ridge

options.label: E
options.html: WNT7a from the dorsal limb ectoderm

items.explanationHtml:
Metanephric mesenchyme secretes glial cell–derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), which binds the RET receptor tyrosine kinase on the ureteric bud and drives its outgrowth and branching. Loss of this signalling causes renal agenesis or hypoplasia, and variants in the pathway are found in some children with congenital kidney anomalies. RET is also the gene mutated in Hirschsprung disease and MEN2.

Takeaway: GDNF from the metanephric mesenchyme acting on RET in the ureteric bud starts kidney development.

whyNot.A: Anti-Müllerian hormone from Sertoli cells causes regression of the paramesonephric ducts.
whyNot.B: FGF8 from the apical ectodermal ridge drives proximal-to-distal limb outgrowth.
whyNot.D: Sonic hedgehog from the notochord and floor plate patterns the ventral neural tube.
whyNot.E: WNT7a sets the dorsal-ventral axis of the limb.

items.objective: Name the GDNF–RET signal that induces ureteric bud outgrowth.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy has had several episodes of dull left flank pain and nausea, each beginning about an hour after he drinks large volumes of fluid at parties. Between episodes he is well. Ultrasonography during an episode shows marked dilation of the left renal pelvis and calyces, with a normal-calibre left ureter and normal bladder. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.label: C
options.html: Obstruction at the left ureteropelvic junction

items.explanationHtml:
Dilation of the pelvis and calyces with a normal ureter places the obstruction at the ureteropelvic junction. It may come from an intrinsic aperistaltic segment or a crossing lower-pole vessel. A large fluid load overwhelms the narrowed outlet and stretches the pelvis, causing intermittent pain.

Takeaway: hydronephrosis with a normal-calibre ureter means ureteropelvic junction obstruction; pain after fluid loads is typical in older children.

whyNot.A: Obstruction at the ureterovesical junction would dilate the ureter as well (megaureter).
whyNot.B: Reflux dilates the ureter and pelvis together and does not cause pain triggered by drinking.
whyNot.D: Valves affect boys from infancy, distend the bladder and cause bilateral hydronephrosis.
whyNot.E: Retroperitoneal fibrosis affects older adults and narrows the mid ureters, usually on both sides.

items.objective: Localise congenital obstruction to the ureteropelvic junction.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl has been damp at all times since toilet training, although she also voids normally several times a day. Her parents have tried timed voiding without change. Examination shows constant moisture of the perineum. Imaging shows a complete duplication of the right collecting system with a dilated upper-pole moiety. Which of the following best describes the most likely anatomy?

options.label: A
options.html: Lower-pole ureter inserting into the vagina

options.label: B
options.html: Lower-pole ureter inserting laterally in the bladder with reflux

options.label: C
options.html: Upper-pole ureter inserting into the bladder at the trigone

options.label: D
options.html: Upper-pole ureter inserting into the urethra below the sphincter

options.label: E
options.html: Both ureters joining before entering the bladder

items.explanationHtml:
In a complete duplex system, the upper-pole ureter enters lower and more medially than normal and can open outside the bladder. In girls, an opening into the urethra below the sphincter or into the vagina leaks continuously while the bladder, filled by the lower pole and the other kidney, still fills and empties normally.

Takeaway: a girl with continuous wetness despite normal voiding has an ectopic upper-pole ureter opening below the sphincter.

whyNot.A: The lower-pole ureter inserts higher and more laterally, on or above the trigone, and does not open ectopically.
whyNot.B: Lateral insertion with reflux is typical of the lower pole, but reflux causes infection, not continuous dribbling.
whyNot.C: A ureter opening normally into the bladder above the sphincter would not cause constant leakage.
whyNot.E: Joining of the ureters is a partial (incomplete) duplication with a single opening in the normal position.

items.objective: Apply the Weigert-Meyer pattern to explain continuous incontinence in a girl with a duplex system.

items.stemHtml: A routine prenatal ultrasound at 22 weeks shows a normal amount of amniotic fluid, a normal left kidney, and a right flank mass made up of many round, noncommunicating cysts of varying size with no visible renal parenchyma. After birth, a nuclear scan shows no function on the right. If the right kidney were examined microscopically, which of the following findings would be most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Cysts lined by flattened epithelium in a kidney of normal architecture

options.label: B
options.html: Dilated collecting ducts arranged radially at right angles to the capsule

options.label: C
options.html: Primitive tubules surrounded by fibromuscular collars, with islands of cartilage

options.label: D
options.html: Small blue cells forming tubules and blastema with stroma

options.label: E
options.html: Sheets of clear cells in nests separated by delicate vessels

items.explanationHtml:
This is multicystic dysplastic kidney, which results from abnormal interaction between the ureteric bud and the metanephric mesenchyme, often with an atretic ureter. Dysplasia means abnormal tissue differentiation: primitive ducts with fibromuscular collars and islands of cartilage among cysts. A normal opposite kidney explains the normal amniotic fluid.

Takeaway: dysplasia shows primitive ducts and cartilage; unilateral multicystic dysplastic kidney leaves amniotic fluid normal.

whyNot.A: Simple cysts in an otherwise normal kidney are acquired simple renal cysts of adults.
whyNot.B: Radially arranged dilated collecting ducts are the pattern of autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease, which is bilateral and causes oligohydramnios.
whyNot.D: Blastema, tubules and stroma make up nephroblastoma (Wilms tumour), a solid tumour of childhood.
whyNot.E: Nests of clear cells describe clear cell renal cell carcinoma in adults.

items.objective: Recognise the histology and course of multicystic dysplastic kidney.

items.stemHtml: A 6-week-old boy has persistent clear, wet drainage from the umbilicus since the cord separated. The drainage increases when he cries. The fluid's creatinine concentration is many times that of his serum. Persistence of which of the following embryonic structures most likely explains this finding?
items.explanationHtml:
The allantois connects the dome of the bladder to the umbilicus as the urachus, which normally closes into the median umbilical ligament. A patent urachus drains urine (high creatinine) from the umbilicus, more with straining or crying. Partial persistence gives a urachal cyst or sinus, and in adults urachal remnants can give adenocarcinoma at the bladder dome.

Takeaway: urine draining from the umbilicus means a patent urachus, a remnant of the allantois.

whyNot.B: A persistent vitelline duct connects the ileum to the umbilicus and drains meconium or stool, not urine.
whyNot.C: The paramesonephric ducts form the uterine tubes, uterus and upper vagina; they have no connection to the umbilicus.
whyNot.D: The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres and carries blood, not urine.
whyNot.E: Failure of the urorectal septum causes anorectal malformations and fistulas, not umbilical drainage.

items.objective: Identify a patent urachus as a persistent allantoic remnant.

items.stemHtml: A newborn girl has a red, moist plate of bladder mucosa exposed on the lower anterior abdominal wall below a low-set umbilicus. The clitoris is bifid, and radiography shows wide separation of the pubic bones. Failure of which of the following developmental processes most directly caused this anomaly?

options.label: D
options.html: Mesodermal migration into the infraumbilical body wall

options.label: E
options.html: Septation of the cloaca by the urorectal septum

items.explanationHtml:
Bladder exstrophy results when mesoderm fails to migrate between the ectoderm and endoderm of the lower abdominal wall over the cloacal membrane. The unsupported membrane ruptures and exposes the bladder plate, with epispadias and diastasis of the pubic symphysis.

Takeaway: bladder exstrophy is a failure of infraumbilical mesoderm to reinforce the cloacal membrane, with epispadias and pubic diastasis.

whyNot.A: Failed canalisation at the ureteropelvic junction causes hydronephrosis, not an open abdominal wall.
whyNot.B: Failed caudal neuropore closure causes spina bifida.
whyNot.C: Failed fusion of the urethral folds in males causes hypospadias on the ventral penis.
whyNot.E: Failed cloacal septation causes anorectal malformations and persistent cloaca.

items.objective: Explain the embryologic basis of bladder exstrophy.

items.stemHtml: A boy is born at 39 weeks' gestation after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Ultrasonography at 32 weeks showed mild dilation of the left renal pelvis (anteroposterior diameter 9 mm), a normal right kidney, a normal bladder and normal amniotic fluid. He is now 6 hours old, feeding well and voiding with a good stream. Examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan for imaging?

options.label: B
options.html: No imaging unless he develops a UTI

options.label: D
options.html: Renal and bladder ultrasonography after 48 hours of life

items.explanationHtml:
Mild unilateral prenatal pelvic dilation with a normal bladder and normal amniotic fluid is followed up with postnatal ultrasonography after about 48 hours (usually within the first weeks).
